instruction: i need to allocate some space on stack for my local variables (in x86-64 nasm assembly)
output:
Below is a minimal example of how you can allocate space for local variables on the stack in x86-64 assembly using NASM. This example follows the standard System V ABI calling convention on Linux. The key steps are:

• Create a function prologue: push the old base pointer (RBP) and set the new base pointer to RSP.  
• Reserve space by subtracting from RSP.  
• Access local variables as negative offsets from RBP (e.g., [rbp - 8]).  
• Before returning, unwind the stack: add back the reserved space and restore RBP.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
global main          ; We'll define "main" as our entry point for this example

section .text

main:
    ; -- Function prologue --
    ; Save the old base pointer and establish a new one
    push    rbp
    mov     rbp, rsp

    ; Reserve 32 bytes on the stack for local variables
    ; Adjust the number as needed for the size of your local data
    sub     rsp, 32

    ; -- Body of the function --
    ; Example: store an integer 42 at the first 4 bytes of local space
    ; [rbp - 4] is within the space we reserved (32 bytes).
    mov     DWORD [rbp - 4], 42

    ; ... do more work here ...

    ; -- Function epilogue --
    ; Restore the stack pointer and base pointer
    leave       ; equivalent to: mov rsp, rbp / pop rbp
    ret
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation of key points:
• push rbp / mov rbp, rsp  
  This is the typical prologue that sets up a new stack frame so local variables can be accessed using rbp-based addressing.

• sub rsp, 32  
  This reserves 32 bytes of stack space for local variables. You can increase or decrease this number depending on how many bytes you need. Typically, you also want to keep rsp 16-byte aligned when calling other functions.

• mov DWORD [rbp - 4], 42  
  Here, we’re writing the 32-bit value 42 into the location rbp-4, which lies within the 32 bytes just allocated. In general, local variables go at negative offsets from rbp.

• leave / ret  
  The leave instruction effectively undoes the function prologue, restoring rbp and setting rsp to the old rbp. ret then returns to the caller.

With this pattern, you can allocate as many bytes as necessary for your local variables. Just remember to keep track of alignment requirements (for example, ensuring 16-byte alignment before calls) and to release the stack space properly before returning.

instruction: Write a function in PPC64 to load the GOT and call a function in the GOT
output:
Below is a minimal PPC64 (ELFv2‐style) assembly example that demonstrates loading the GOT/TOC pointer, retrieving a function pointer from the GOT, and then calling that function.  In this example, we call a function named external_function that is assumed to be linked elsewhere (e.g., in another object or library).  Note that details vary depending on ABI (ELFv1 vs. ELFv2) and whether the code is position‐independent, so be sure to assemble/link consistently.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
	.text
	.machine ppc64le               # or .machine ppc64 if big-endian
	.globl myfunc
	.type  myfunc, @function

myfunc:
	# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
	# 1) Set up r2 (TOC pointer).  Typically, the compiler and/or linker
	#    generate similar instructions automatically if building position-
	#    independent code.  The @ha/@l relocations compute high-adj/low parts
	#    of (.TOC. - myfunc).
	# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
	addis   r2, r12, (.TOC.-myfunc)@ha
	addi    r2, r2, (.TOC.-myfunc)@l

	# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
	# 2) Load the address of the external function from the GOT.  The
	#    “@got” relocation tells the linker that we want the entry for
	#    external_function in the Global Offset Table, and we add r2 (the TOC).
	# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
	ld      r12, external_function@got(r2)

	# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
	# 3) Transfer control to the function:
	#    - mtctr r12 loads the address into the count register.
	#    - bctrl calls the function in CTR and saves the return address in LR.
	# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
	mtctr   r12
	bctrl

	# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
	# 4) Return to the caller.  bctrl has set LR, so we can just return.
	# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
	blr

	.size myfunc, .-myfunc
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation:

• r2 is conventionally the TOC (Table Of Contents) pointer on ppc64 ELFv2, which effectively serves as the GOT pointer for dynamic references.  
• The addis/addi pair calculates (TOC base) relative to this function.  
• “external_function@got(r2)” loads the function’s address pointer from the GOT.  
• mtctr r12 moves that address into the count register, and bctrl performs the actual branch‐and‐link.  
• Upon return, blr uses the link register to return to the caller.

When assembling, ensure your toolchain is configured for the ppc64 or ppc64le target, and link against objects or libraries that define the external_function symbol. If you are mixing C code and assembly, also ensure compile/link flags (such as -fPIC) match your usage of GOT/TOC.

instruction: When training my neural network, I can get a loss below 4.5 at 10,000 iterations. The latest attempt includes trying batch sizes of 512, 1024, and 2048 while keeping the block size  at a 4. All of this is done in the context of nanoGPT. It's worth noting that when I ran a batch size of 12 and a block size of 1024, I managed to get the loss down to 4.32 after 10,000 iterations. In your opinion and experience, what steps can I take in order to reduce the loss? Please keep in mind that my video card has 12GB of RAM and the vocabulary is made up of 20,000 words. Each sentence is made up of exactly four tokens. Do you have any suggestions how I could improve the neural network, please?
output:
Below are several observations and suggestions to consider when trying to reduce your model’s loss in nanoGPT, given a 12 GB GPU and a vocabulary of 20,000 words, where each sentence consists of exactly four tokens:

1) Re-evaluate the block size.  
   • Since your sentences are only four tokens long, a large block size (e.g., 1024) may not be giving you meaningful additional context—unless you are concatenating many four-token sentences into a single context window.  
   • If your data truly has no long-range dependencies (each record is 4 tokens, entirely self-contained), you may not gain much from a big context length.  
   • On the other hand, if your dataset is structured so that multiple four-token sentences could form a coherent sequence, then grouping them into a larger block can help the model learn transitions between consecutive sentences. But if they are all disjoint, a block size of 4 (or a multiple near 4) is more natural.

2) Tune your learning rate (and schedule).  
   • Often, the single most important hyperparameter is the learning rate. If your loss plateaus or doesn’t improve much, try lowering it (e.g., half or even 1/10) or use a learning-rate schedule with warm-up and decay.  
   • Watch for instability (loss spikes or NaNs) if the learning rate is too high.

3) Adjust your batch size strategy.  
   • Very large batch sizes can sometimes slow down convergence if your dataset isn’t very large or if the model is struggling to generalize.  
   • However, using a batch size that is too small can lead to noisy gradients. If GPU memory is an issue, experiment with gradient accumulation to achieve an “effective” large batch size without storing everything at once.  
   • Try a moderate batch size (like 64, 128, or 256) or use the largest batch size that comfortably fits and see if it helps convergence.

4) Ensure the model capacity matches the task.  
   • For a 20k vocabulary, you want to make sure the model embed dimension is high enough to represent the vocabulary effectively, but not so large that it is unwieldy for your GPU or your dataset size.  
   • The same applies to the number of layers and heads. If the model is too shallow, it may not learn rich representations; if it is too large, you may not be able to train long enough (or with a large enough batch) before running out of memory.  
   • Try a moderate-sized transformer (e.g., 6–12 layers, hidden size in the hundreds range) and confirm that you can train for enough steps without either overfitting or running out of GPU memory.

5) Consider the amount and variety of training data.  
   • If your vocabulary is large (20k), but each sentence is only four tokens, the raw amount of text diversity may be limited.  
   • If possible, gather more data or ensure your existing dataset has enough variety and coverage of tokens.  
   • Make sure your dataset is shuffled well and that no undesired duplicates or data-quality issues are present.

6) Optimize other hyperparameters.  
   • Try different weight decay (L2 regularization) values. A small amount of weight decay can help generalization.  
   • Experiment with dropout if overfitting is an issue.  
   • Make sure you are initializing AdamW (or Adam) with recommended defaults (β1=0.9, β2=0.95 or 0.999, etc.) and that your betas or epsilon are not set to unusual values.

7) Look at your tokenizer strategy.  
   • Double-check that the 20k vocabulary is efficiently covering your data. If each four-token sentence uses a wide range of tokens, you might not be giving the model a chance to generalize well.  
   • If possible, confirm that your tokens actually match your data distribution (e.g., using a subword tokenizer like BPE or SentencePiece) and that you aren’t wasting many tokens on rarely occurring words or inconsistent segmentation.

8) Train for more steps or use early stopping carefully.  
   • If you see a consistent downward trend in the loss even after 10,000 iterations, consider training longer. Sometimes the loss curve continues to drop slowly over more iterations.  
   • Track validation loss to avoid overfitting. If training and validation losses diverge, consider adding regularization or lowering the learning rate.

9) Employ gradient checkpointing if memory is tight.  
   • If your model is large or your batch size is constrained by memory, gradient checkpointing can free up memory at the cost of extra compute. This often lets you use a slightly larger model or bigger batch sizes.

10) Keep an eye on data preprocessing and random seed.  
   • Small mistakes in data preprocessing (e.g., off-by-one in token indices, misaligned embeddings) can hamper performance. Double-check your preprocessing pipeline.  
   • Sometimes re-seeding or re-initing the model can change early training dynamics, so do controlled experiments to confirm consistent runs.

Putting it all together, the most direct actions to try would be:
• Use a moderately sized batch (or use gradient accumulation to simulate a larger batch).  
• Tune the learning rate and learning-rate schedule carefully (e.g., a smaller peak learning rate than you currently have, plus slower decay).  
• Check that your model size (number of layers, hidden dimension) is neither too small (underfitting) nor too large (memory constraints, difficulty converging).  
• Confirm that your tokenizer is well-suited to your data distribution and is not artificially inflating perplexity.  
• Train for a sufficient number of iterations and watch for a continuing downward trend in loss.

Experimentation with these configurations—while monitoring both training and validation losses—should help you push your loss below 4.3 and beyond. Good luck!

output:
Below is a basic Python script demonstrating how to use yfinance to retrieve daily stock data (for example, Apple), store it into a Pandas DataFrame, and then plot the closing prices:

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
import yfinance as yf
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Define the ticker (e.g., Apple)
ticker_symbol = "AAPL"

# 2. Download daily data for the last year
df = yf.download(ticker_symbol, period="1y", interval="1d")

# 3. Plot the closing prices
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(df.index, df["Close"], label="Close Price")
plt.title(f"{ticker_symbol} Stock Price")
plt.xlabel("Date")
plt.ylabel("Price (USD)")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation:
• yfinance provides convenient methods to fetch stock data from Yahoo Finance.
• yf.download(...) returns a DataFrame with columns such as Open, High, Low, Close, Adj Close, and Volume.
• period="1y" fetches data for the past year; interval="1d" provides daily data. You can adjust these parameters to your needs.
• Matplotlib is used to create a simple line plot of the Close column over time.

instruction: Using pandas-ta, I have forex data and an 'EMA50' column. I want to detect where the close price crosses over the 'EMA50' value.
output:
Below is a simple pattern you can use to detect when price crosses above (or below) the EMA50 in a Pandas DataFrame. The key idea is to compare today’s relationship (close > EMA50) with yesterday’s relationship (close ≤ EMA50), using shift(1) to access prior values.

Example:

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Suppose your DataFrame is named df and contains columns: "Close" and "EMA50".

import pandas as pd

# 1) Identify where price crosses ABOVE EMA50:
df["Cross_Above"] = (
    (df["Close"] > df["EMA50"]) &            # today's close is above the EMA
    (df["Close"].shift(1) <= df["EMA50"].shift(1))  # yesterday's close was at or below the EMA
)

# 2) (Optional) Identify where price crosses BELOW EMA50:
df["Cross_Below"] = (
    (df["Close"] < df["EMA50"]) &
    (df["Close"].shift(1) >= df["EMA50"].shift(1))
)

# The resulting Series (True/False) indicates the exact rows where crossovers occur.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation:

• (df["Close"] > df["EMA50"]) checks if today’s close is above the 50-period EMA.  
• (df["Close"].shift(1) <= df["EMA50"].shift(1)) checks if yesterday’s close was at or below its 50-period EMA.  
• By combining these two conditions with &, you get True precisely on the row where a crossover from below to above happens.  
• You can do the reverse for crosses below by flipping the comparisons.

If you are using the pandas-ta library, you can also explore ta.cross() directly (e.g., ta.cross(df["Close"], df["EMA50"])) to generate crossover signals in a similar fashion.

I am migrating from MacOS Mojave running Safari 14 to a new Mac running Safari 17 under MacOS Sonoma. I want Safari on my new Mac to automatically open with all the tabs open on my old Mac. Note that Safari 14 does not support iCloud tabs, and that I do *not* want to have to manually open each tab as I have hundreds of them!
output:
Unfortunately, because Safari 14 on Mojave does not offer iCloud syncing for open tabs, the only practical way to preserve your hundreds of open tabs (so that they re‐open automatically on the new Mac) is to bring over Safari’s internal “session” data directly. The most reliable method is to use Apple’s Migration Assistant to move your entire user account (including Safari data) from the old Mac to the new one. Here is the general approach:

1) Quit Safari on the old Mac first.  
   • This ensures Safari writes out its current session—i.e., all open tabs—to disk.

2) Use Migration Assistant on the new Mac.  
   • On the new Mac (running macOS Sonoma), open Migration Assistant (in /Applications/Utilities).  
   • Connect the old Mac via Target Disk Mode, network, Time Machine backup, or however you prefer.  
   • In Migration Assistant, select the old Mac (or its backup) as the source, then choose your user account and Safari data to transfer.

3) Log in on the new Mac and launch Safari.  
   • Because the session data was transferred, Safari on the new Mac should pick up right where the old Mac left off, including all windows and tabs that were open.  

What if you’ve already set up the new Mac?  
• You can still run Migration Assistant later: it will bring over the user account (merging or creating a new account). Make sure you do not open Safari on the new Mac until after the migration, just to reduce the chance of overwriting the session files.  

Can you just copy files instead of using Migration Assistant?  
• In principle you could manually copy the various Safari library files (the session/state files as well as bookmarks, history, etc.) from ~/Library/Safari on the old Mac to the new Mac. However, Safari’s internal file formats can change between versions—especially going from Safari 14 (Mojave) to Safari 17 (Sonoma)—and a mismatch could break your Safari profile or corrupt data.  
• Migration Assistant handles these version transitions more gracefully by correctly mapping and upgrading the Safari data.  

Bottom line:  
• Apple’s Migration Assistant is by far the safest way to preserve your open tabs across such a big jump in Safari/macOS versions. Once you transfer via Migration Assistant (with Safari shut down on the old Mac), you should be able to open Safari on the new Mac and see all your hundreds of tabs just as they were.

instruction:
Find a fix for this bug : 
```This model maximum context length is 2048 tokens. However, your messages resulted in over 2364 tokens.```
output:
When you see the error “This model maximum context length is 2048 tokens. However, your messages resulted in over 2364 tokens,” it means the text you’re sending to the model is too long for it to handle in a single request. Here are some ways to fix or work around this:

1. Shorten the prompt (or conversation):
   – Remove any extraneous detail in your prompt or conversation history.  
   – Summarize previous messages before passing them to the model so that only the essential context is preserved.

2. Split the conversation:
   – If you have a lengthy text to analyze or a string of messages to process, break them into smaller chunks.  
   – Send the text in multiple requests, each falling within the model’s token limit.

3. Use query-based summarization when needed:
   – Instead of passing the entire conversation, first summarize older parts of the conversation and then include the summarized text as context.  
   – This reduces token usage while preserving the important context.

4. Switch to a model with a larger context window:
   – If your use case often involves large blocks of text, consider using a model that supports a bigger context window (e.g., 4096 tokens or higher). This might involve switching from one GPT-based model to another with expanded limits.

Summary:
To fix the error, ensure that your total request (including the conversation history and your new prompt) stays under the model’s token limit by removing unnecessary information, summarizing prior content, splitting the request into multiple parts, or using a larger-context model if available.

Tasks:

   – Initialize a new Node.js project (npm init).  
   – Install core dependencies (express, dotenv, etc.).  
   – Configure ESLint/Prettier for code formatting and linting.  
   – Create a basic Express server with a health-check endpoint (GET /health).

2. React Application Setup  
   – Use create-react-app or Vite to scaffold a new React app.  
   – Install necessary dependencies (React Router, Axios, etc.).  
   – Create a basic main page with an “Under Construction” message.  
   – Configure environment variables for development (e.g., REACT_APP_API_URL).

3. Project Folder Structure Definition  
   – server/  
     ├─ config/  
     ├─ controllers/  
     ├─ models/  
     ├─ routes/  
     ├─ middlewares/  
     ├─ index.js  
   – client/  
     ├─ src/  
       ├─ components/  
       ├─ pages/  
       ├─ redux/ or hooks/  
       ├─ App.js  
     ├─ public/  

4. Security & Best Practices Baseline  
   – Add helmet and cors in Express.  
   – Create a .env file (store sensitive data like DB credentials).

Ticket #2: Database Schema & Migrations
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Goal: Define a robust SQL schema to store user accounts, device inventory, and support role-based access. Implement migrations to keep schema under version control.

Tasks:
1. Choose & Configure the ORM/Query Builder  
   – Install Sequelize or TypeORM.  
   – Configure the DB connection in config/database.js (or equivalent).  
   – Update .env with DB_HOST, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD, DB_NAME.

2. Create Database Models  
   – User model/table: id, name, email, password (hashed), role (USER/STAFF/ADMIN), createdAt, updatedAt.  
   – Device model/table: id, name, reference, quantity, createdAt, updatedAt (extendable for mechanical device details).

3. Write & Run Migrations  
   – For User table creation.  
   – For Device table creation.  
   – Additional migrations if needed (e.g., logs, user profile details).

4. Seed Initial Data (optional for testing)  
   – Insert a default admin user (with hashed password) into the User table.  
   – Insert a few sample devices to test relationships.

5. Testing the Connection  
   – Write a test script to ensure the DB connections and models work properly.  
   – Possibly implement a basic GET /devices endpoint to fetch all devices as a test.

Ticket #3: Authentication & Role-Based Authorization
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Goal: Implement secure user authentication using JSON Web Tokens (JWT) or session-based, and enforce role-based authorization across different routes.

Tasks:
1. Configure Authentication  
   – Install jsonwebtoken or passport-jwt.  
   – Create an authentication service to handle sign-up, login, token issuance, and token verification.  
   – Store hashed passwords using bcrypt during user registration.

2. Generate & Validate Tokens  
   – Write a login route (POST /auth/login) to accept credentials and respond with a signed JWT.  
   – Create a middleware that verifies JWT on protected routes.

3. Role-Based Authorization Middleware  
   – Add a middleware that checks user role from the verified token (e.g., check if role === 'STAFF' or 'ADMIN').  
   – Apply appropriate role checks to relevant routes:
     – USER role: read all devices, update individual records.  
     – STAFF role: also can create new device records and submit bulk updates.  
     – ADMIN role: can create or eliminate database fields and manage users.

4. Refresh Token (Optional)  
   – If needed for security or usability, implement a refresh token flow to keep sessions active.

5. Frontend Integration  
   – Create signup/login forms in React.  
   – Store JWT in secure httpOnly cookies or handle it carefully in local storage with caution.  
   – Implement React Router guards to redirect users who are not authenticated or unauthorized for certain routes.

Ticket #4: CRUD Operations for Devices
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Goal: Provide endpoints and frontend pages for users/staff to create, read, update, and (for staff) do bulk updates, with proper validations.

Tasks:
1. Backend CRUD Endpoints  
   – GET /devices – fetch all devices (accessible by all roles).  
   – GET /devices/:id – fetch a specific device (accessible by all roles).  
   – POST /devices – add a new device (staff/admin only).  
   – PUT /devices/:id – update an existing device (user for own updates, staff/admin for any).  
   – DELETE /devices/:id – if applicable, staff/admin can remove a device (or soft delete).

2. Bulk Updates Endpoint  
   – POST /devices/bulk – staff can submit an array of device updates in a single request.
   – Validate the data format to ensure no malicious entries.

3. Validation & Error Handling  
   – Use express-validator or equivalent for input validation (e.g., device name, reference not empty, quantity is numeric).  
   – Implement robust error handling with consistent error messages.

4. Frontend Implementation  
   – Create React pages/components for listing devices, creating a new device, bulk edit page, and editing individual devices.  
   – Use protected routes in React Router for staff-only pages.

5. Security Checks  
   – Ensure that only authorized roles can access the relevant endpoints.  
   – Log actions (e.g., device creation, updates) if needed for auditing.

Ticket #5: Bulk Updates & Admin Management
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Goal: Complete and refine staff’s bulk update features, and empower admins to manage users and database fields securely.

Tasks:
1. Staff Bulk Updates Refinement  
   – Confirm staff can send multiple objects (devices) in a single request to POST /devices/bulk.  
   – Implement transaction-based updates with the ORM to ensure atomicity (all or nothing if an error occurs).

2. Admin User Management  
   – Create endpoints for admin:  
     – GET /admin/users – list all users.  
     – POST /admin/users – create new user with specific role.  
     – PUT /admin/users/:id – update user role/password.  
     – DELETE /admin/users/:id – remove user from the system.  

3. Admin Database Fields Management  
   – Provide an endpoint to add new columns to Devices table (or create new tables in advanced scenarios).  
   – Provide an endpoint to remove fields (migration approach or a simpler dynamic approach).  
   – Ensure these operations are heavily authenticated and authorized for admin role only.

4. Frontend Admin Dashboard  
   – Implement an Admin UI for user management (list, invite new user, update roles, remove user).  
   – Implement an Admin UI for managing database fields or schemas (unless a separate tool like pgAdmin is used — but as a requirement, you can provide a minimal interface).

5. Quality Assurance & Final Security Checks  
   – Conduct an integration test for bulk updates.  
   – Perform user acceptance testing for admin features.  
   – Validate security with respect to injection, cross-site scripting, etc.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. CONCLUSION & BEST PRACTICES
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

• Environment Segregation: Keep separate .env files for development, testing, and production.  
• Data Security: Never store passwords in plain text. Always use bcrypt or Argon2 for password hashing.  
• Threat Protection: Use helmet and cors configured properly. Validate all requests with express-validator.  
• Logging & Monitoring: Implement a logging system (Winston/Pino) and track critical actions in logs for auditing.  
• Scalability: Deploy behind a reverse proxy (e.g., NGINX) or use a container orchestration platform (Kubernetes or Docker Swarm).  
• Code Organization: Maintain a clear MVC or layered architecture in Node.js and a consistent folder structure in React.  
• Automation & Continuous Integration: Use GitHub Actions or other CI/CD pipelines to run tests, lint code, and deploy automatically.

With this architecture plan, helper libraries, sprint tickets, and the associated tasks, you’ll have a clear roadmap to build a secure, scalable mechanical device inventory management application with Node.js, SQL, and React.

instruction: I need to connect a list of FBIDs found in support tickets (the dim_tier1_job_final table) to a list of page IDs found in a target list. Unfortunately, our support tickets typically don't include a page ID. How can I connect these two lists of data in Daiquery?
output:
In Daiquery, the usual way to link “object” FBIDs from a Tier‐1 table (like dim_tier1_job_final) to Page IDs is to run the FBIDs through a table that recognizes them as Pages and returns the Page ID. In other words, you’ll need a “bridge” step where you map each FBID to its corresponding Page ID before you can join against your target list on page_id.

Below is the typical workflow:

1) Identify which column in dim_tier1_job_final contains the relevant object FBID   
   • Often this is something like “object_fbid” or “page_fbid” or “job_fbid,” depending on the table.  

2) Join that FBID to a table or dimension that can tell you “This FBID is a Page, and its canonical page_id is …”  
   • For example, “dim_page” or “dim_fb_object” or another dimension used in the pipeline that resolves FBIDs to Page IDs (the exact name of this table can differ by product area or pipeline).  

3) Once you have the Page IDs from the dimension table, you can do a second join to your target list using page_id.  

In practice, your query might look like this (pseudo‐SQL):

WITH tier1_jobs AS (
  SELECT 
    job_id,
    object_fbid
  FROM databasename.dim_tier1_job_final
  WHERE <filters>
),
fbid_to_page AS (
  SELECT
    fbid AS page_fbid,    -- or object_fbid, whichever the dimension calls it
    page_id
  FROM databasename.dim_page  -- or whichever dimension has page mappings
  WHERE <filters>
)
SELECT
  t1.job_id,
  p.page_id,
  target.*
FROM tier1_jobs t1
JOIN fbid_to_page p
  ON t1.object_fbid = p.page_fbid
JOIN target_list target
  ON p.page_id = target.page_id;

In that pattern:
• tier1_jobs pulls the relevant FBIDs from the Tier‐1 table.  
• fbid_to_page maps those FBIDs onto canonical page_ids.  
• You then join again to your target_list on page_id.

By following that “FBID → dimension with page_id → target_list on page_id” chain, you can resolve the support‐ticket FBIDs to Page IDs and connect them to your target list.

Joe the trainer has two solo workout plans that he offers his clients: Plan A and Plan B. Each client does either one or the other (not both). On Monday there were 9 clients who did Plan A and 7 who did Plan B. On Tuesday there were 3 clients who did Plan A and 5 who did Plan B. Joe trained his Monday clients for a total of 12 hours and his Tuesday clients for a total of 6 hours. How long does each of the workout plans last?     length of each plan A workout?                 length of each plan B workout
output:
Let x be the duration (in hours) of Plan A and y be the duration of Plan B. From the problem:

• On Monday (9 clients on Plan A and 7 on Plan B), total training = 12 hours:  
  9x + 7y = 12  

• On Tuesday (3 clients on Plan A and 5 on Plan B), total training = 6 hours:  
  3x + 5y = 6  

Solve the second equation for x:  
  3x = 6 − 5y  →  x = (6 − 5y)/3  

Substitute into the first equation:  
  9⋅((6 − 5y)/3) + 7y = 12  
  3(6 − 5y) + 7y = 12  
  18 − 15y + 7y = 12  
  18 − 8y = 12  
  −8y = −6  
  y = 6/8 = 3/4  

Then substitute y = 3/4 back to find x:  
  x = (6 − 5⋅(3/4))/3 = (6 − 15/4)/3 = (24/4 − 15/4)/3 = (9/4) ÷ 3 = 9/12 = 3/4  

Hence, each Plan A workout and each Plan B workout lasts 3/4 of an hour, i.e., 45 minutes.  

Answer:  
• Length of each Plan A workout: ¾ hour (45 minutes)  
• Length of each Plan B workout: ¾ hour (45 minutes)

instruction: show me the steps to build an invoice app using phython
output:
Below is a high-level outline of how you can build a simple invoice app in Python. The example uses the Flask web framework (for a web-based application), an SQLite database (via SQLAlchemy), and a PDF generation library (ReportLab). This outline can be adapted to other frameworks or libraries depending on your preference. ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 1. Plan Your Features and Data Model ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── • Decide which fields your invoices will include (e.g., invoice number, date, client information, list of items, prices, totals). • Decide whether your app needs user authentication, multiple clients, multiple items per invoice, taxes, discounts, etc. • Plan how you want to generate the final invoice (PDF, HTML template, etc.). ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 2. Set Up Your Environment ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 1. Install Python 3 (if you haven’t already). 2. Create and activate a virtual environment (recommended): python -m venv venv source venv/bin/activate # On Linux/macOS venv\Scripts\activate # On Windows 3. Install the necessary Python libraries: pip install flask sqlalchemy reportlab ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 3. Define Your Project Structure ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── A typical Flask project might look like this: invoice_app/ │ ├── app.py # Main Flask application ├── models.py # Database models (SQLAlchemy) ├── forms.py # (Optional) Flask-WTF forms ├── requirements.txt # List of dependencies ├── templates/ # HTML templates (if you use Flask’s render_template) │ ├── base.html │ ├── create_invoice.html │ ├── list_invoices.html │ └── ... └── static/ # CSS, JavaScript, images ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 4. Initialize a Flask App (app.py) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── from flask import Flask, render_template from flask_sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemy app = Flask(__name__) # Configure Flask & SQLAlchemy app.config['SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI'] = 'sqlite:///invoices.db' app.config['SQLALCHEMY_TRACK_MODIFICATIONS'] = False db = SQLAlchemy(app) # Import models after db is defined from models import Invoice, Item # You will define these in models.py # Simple home route @app.route('/') def index(): return "Welcome to the Invoice App" if __name__ == '__main__': app.run(debug=True) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 5. Create Database Models (models.py) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── from app import db class Invoice(db.Model): __tablename__ = 'invoices' id = db.Column(db.Integer, primary_key=True) invoice_number = db.Column(db.String(50), unique=True, nullable=False) client_name = db.Column(db.String(100), nullable=False) date_created = db.Column(db.DateTime, nullable=False) # One-to-many relationship with Item items = db.relationship('Item', backref='invoice', lazy=True) class Item(db.Model): __tablename__ = 'items' id = db.Column(db.Integer, primary_key=True) description = db.Column(db.String(200), nullable=False) quantity = db.Column(db.Integer, default=1) price = db.Column(db.Float, nullable=False) invoice_id = db.Column(db.Integer, db.ForeignKey('invoices.id'), nullable=False) Note: You can expand your models to store more information (taxes, discounts, statuses, etc.). ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 6. Create and Populate the Database ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── In a Python shell or a separate script, initialize the database: from app import db db.create_all() You can add some test data manually or via your app routes: from models import Invoice, Item from datetime import datetime invoice = Invoice( invoice_number="INV-1001", client_name="John Doe", date_created=datetime.now() ) db.session.add(invoice) db.session.commit() item1 = Item( description="Widget A", quantity=3, price=10.00, invoice_id=invoice.id ) db.session.add(item1) db.session.commit() ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 7. Create Routes to List and Create Invoices ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Below are examples of how you might add routes in app.py to: • Display all invoices (“/invoices”) • Display a form to create a new invoice (“/create_invoice”) • Process the form data and store it in the database from flask import Flask, render_template, request, redirect, url_for from datetime import datetime from app import app, db from models import Invoice, Item @app.route('/invoices') def list_invoices(): invoices = Invoice.query.all() return render_template('list_invoices.html', invoices=invoices) @app.route('/create_invoice', methods=['GET', 'POST']) def create_invoice(): if request.method == 'POST': invoice_number = request.form['invoice_number'] client_name = request.form['client_name'] # Create the Invoice object new_invoice = Invoice( invoice_number=invoice_number, client_name=client_name, date_created=datetime.now() ) db.session.add(new_invoice) db.session.commit() # Optionally, add Items to the invoice here or on a separate page return redirect(url_for('list_invoices')) return render_template('create_invoice.html') ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 8. Generate PDF Invoices with ReportLab ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Use the ReportLab library to generate PDFs. You might create a new route “/invoice_pdf/” that returns the PDF. Install ReportLab (if not already): pip install reportlab Then in app.py, create a route to generate the PDF: from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import LETTER from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas from flask import make_response @app.route('/invoice_pdf/') def invoice_pdf(invoice_id): invoice = Invoice.query.get_or_404(invoice_id) # Create a in-memory PDF buffer from io import BytesIO buffer = BytesIO() pdf = canvas.Canvas(buffer, pagesize=LETTER) # Write invoice header details pdf.drawString(50, 750, f"Invoice Number: {invoice.invoice_number}") pdf.drawString(50, 730, f"Client Name: {invoice.client_name}") pdf.drawString(50, 710, f"Date: {invoice.date_created.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')}") # Table-like structure for items y_position = 650 for item in invoice.items: line = f"{item.description} (Qty: {item.quantity}) @ ${item.price}" pdf.drawString(50, y_position, line) y_position -= 20 # Close the PDF object and get the value of the BytesIO buffer pdf.showPage() pdf.save() pdf_data = buffer.getvalue() buffer.close() # Return the PDF as a response response = make_response(pdf_data) response.headers.set('Content-Type', 'application/pdf') response.headers.set('Content-Disposition', 'attachment', filename=f"invoice_{invoice.id}.pdf") return response ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 9. Create HTML Templates (Optional) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── If you intend to use HTML templates, create templates in the templates folder: • templates/list_invoices.html • templates/create_invoice.html • etc. Example list_invoices.html: --------------------------- Invoices

Invoices

Create New Invoice
    {% for inv in invoices %}
  • Invoice #{{ inv.invoice_number }} - {{ inv.client_name }} [Download PDF]
    • {% endfor %}
Example create_invoice.html: ---------------------------- Create Invoice

Create Invoice





──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 10. Run and Test Your App ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 1. Make sure you have created your database tables (db.create_all()). 2. Start the Flask development server: flask run or python app.py 3. Visit http://127.0.0.1:5000 in your browser. ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Additional Tips ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── • Validation & Security: You’ll want to validate user input (especially if you expose this beyond local development). Consider using Flask-WTF or other form validators. • Authentication & Authorization: If multiple users will manage invoices, implement Flask-Login or another auth system. • Deployment: You can run this app on a service like Heroku, AWS, or any other platform that supports Python + Flask. • Advanced PDF Layout: For more sophisticated invoices, you might use ReportLab’s platypus to create tables and style your PDFs, or other Python PDF libraries. ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── With those steps in place, you’ll have a simple but functional invoice application in Python. Tweak and expand as needed—add features for invoice editing, item editing, or advanced styling of PDFs!

instruction: I am expensing airfare costs with my employer, and the reporting software asks me to specify the GST/HST portion of the expense. Reading the invoice for my flight from Toronto, through Montreal, to Las Vegas, I see a base fare (CAD) of 164.99, Total V.A.T/G.S.T/H.S.T. of $15, and Other Taxes of 132.12. The total invoice then sums to 312.11 CAD. I have never seen a bill with 2 tax categories like this and am not sure how the $15 and 132.12 were calculated, and which I should report as GST/HST in my company's expense report. Can you help me better understand how to correctly report the HST on my airfare?
output:
Below is a practical way to think about it for Canadian GST/HST purposes. In short, the line labeled “Total V.A.T/G.S.T/H.S.T.” (the C $15) is the portion of your airfare that represents GST/HST, whereas the “Other Taxes” (the C $132.12) are a collection of air‐travel charges and taxes (airport improvement fees, U.S. transportation or security fees, etc.) that are not “GST/HST.” In other words:

• The C $15 shown on the invoice is the total amount of GST/HST the airline is charging you.  
• The C $132.12 is a combination of non‐GST/HST fees/taxes (e.g., airport improvement fees, security charges, U.S. customs fees).  

Hence, if your employer’s expense software specifically asks for the “GST/HST portion” of the airfare, you should enter C $15. The rest of the taxes and fees (C $132.12) are not GST/HST and should not be reported as such.  

Why the GST/HST is “only” C $15:  
• Flights between Canada and most international destinations (e.g., the U.S.) are generally zero‐rated under GST/HST law—meaning no Canadian GST/HST applies to the portion of the flight that travels internationally.  
• Only the portion of the airfare that is for travel within Canada (e.g., Toronto to Montreal) is subject to GST/HST, and that results in a smaller tax charge than 13% on your entire fare would suggest.  
• Airlines typically show that Canadian tax portion in one sum labeled “GST/HST” (or sometimes “VAT/GST/HST”), which is how you end up with just C $15 of tax on the invoice instead of 13% of the entire base fare.

If you need a more detailed breakdown, the airline could provide the fare split for domestic vs. international sections, but for expensing in Canada, it is usual to rely on the invoice’s stated “Total V.A.T/G.S.T/H.S.T.” amount (in this case, C $15) when reporting and recovering GST/HST.

instruction: Act as Chief Information Officer and write 3 S.M.A.R.T. goals on creating an IT Incident response plan with detailed table top exercises over the next 6 months.
output:
Below are three S.M.A.R.T. (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) goals focused on creating and refining an IT Incident Response Plan along with conducting detailed tabletop exercises over the next six months.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
GOAL 1: Development of a Comprehensive IT Incident Response Plan
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Specific: Create a written IT Incident Response Plan that outlines clear roles, responsibilities, escalation paths, and communication protocols for all critical systems and data assets.  
• Measurable: The plan will consist of a minimum of 10 essential sections (e.g., incident identification and classification, containment, eradication, recovery, communication, post-incident review, etc.), each reviewed and approved by all relevant stakeholders.  
• Achievable: Utilize existing security frameworks (e.g., NIST, ISO) and collaborate with key departments (IT, Legal, HR, etc.) to gather the necessary requirements.  
• Relevant: Ensures organizational readiness by specifying detailed procedures to prevent, detect, respond to, and recover from cyber and technical incidents.  
• Time-bound: Complete and secure final approval for the plan within three months (by the end of the third month of the six-month window).  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
GOAL 2: Conduct Monthly Tabletop Exercises and Assess Readiness
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Specific: Schedule and execute monthly tabletop exercises that simulate various cybersecurity threats (e.g., ransomware, phishing campaigns, system outages), ensuring cross-functional participation (IT, Legal, PR, HR, etc.).  
• Measurable: Hold six total sessions (one per month), documenting three key performance indicators (KPIs) for each exercise, such as incident identification time, communication effectiveness, and recovery steps.  
• Achievable: Use scenario-driven templates and expert facilitators to ensure each exercise is thorough and tailored to the most relevant threats, with dedicated post-exercise evaluations and lessons learned.  
• Relevant: Enhances the organization’s incident detection and response capability by testing and refining the newly developed Incident Response Plan.  
• Time-bound: Conclude the final (sixth) tabletop exercise by the end of the six-month period, incorporating an after-action review that compares progress across all exercises.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
GOAL 3: Reduce Average Incident Response and Containment Time
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Specific: Streamline detection, communication, and remediation processes to reduce the average incident response and containment time by 30%.  
• Measurable: Track baseline response time (as established prior to plan implementation) against monthly improvements, aiming to shift from a baseline of, for example, 120 minutes to 84 minutes or less.  
• Achievable: Implement improved alerting rules, update escalation procedures, and provide targeted training for the IT security team to optimize efficiency.  
• Relevant: Directly ties into protecting organizational data and systems by ensuring incidents are contained swiftly, minimizing business impact and financial risk.  
• Time-bound: Achieve the 30% reduction by the end of the six-month period, with quarterly checkpoints at months three and six to measure interim progress.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
By focusing on these three S.M.A.R.T. goals, the organization will develop a robust, tested, and continuously improved Incident Response Plan, supported by thorough tabletop exercises. These efforts will collectively enhance the company’s security posture and incident readiness over the designated six-month timeframe.

instruction: how can i use css flexbox to put an image on the same line as a paragraph and have the paragraph automatically format itself around the top and bottom of the picture
output:
Flexbox is great for aligning separate “blocks” side by side, but it does not replicate the classic text‐wrapping behavior you get from floats (where paragraphs flow around an image). In Flexbox, each flex item is laid out as its own box, so text will never wrap tightly around an inline image the way floats do. If you truly need the text to flow around (above and below) the image, you should use float or shape-outside. Below are two approaches, depending on what you need: ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 1) Using Flexbox (simple side-by-side, no text wrapping under the image) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── This approach will place your image and paragraph side by side, but the text will not flow under (around) the image. Instead, the paragraph will appear as one block. For many layouts, this is enough:

This paragraph sits in its own flex-item. If the paragraph is longer than the image, it will simply extend below on the right side, rather than wrapping around the image.

CSS: .flex-container { display: flex; align-items: flex-start; /* Ensures items align at the top edge */ gap: 1rem; /* Adds space between items */ } img { max-width: 200px; /* Example width control for the image */ height: auto; } ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 2) Using float (text wrapping around the image) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── To have the paragraph “wrap” around the image’s top/bottom (the classic newspaper column effect), float the image instead:

This paragraph will wrap around the floated image, automatically filling any available space to its right at the top. Once the paragraph extends below the image, it will occupy the full width of the container.

Additional paragraphs continue to flow around the image if there is still vertical space beside it.

With float: left (and some margin so the text isn’t right against the image), the text automatically flows around the top and bottom of the picture. ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Summary ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── • Flexbox is ideal for laying out discrete blocks in a row or column, but it does not allow text to wrap around an image the way floating does. • If you truly need text to flow around the image (above, beside, and below), you must use float or shape-outside, not pure Flexbox.

instruction: Devise a way to parse the dataframe in python using a bytestream without actually downloading the whole code
output:
Below is a general pattern you can use to parse data incrementally from an HTTP bytestream (e.g., a large CSV file) into a pandas DataFrame without first downloading the entire file to disk. The key idea is to use requests in streaming mode and feed the incoming chunks line-by-line to either Python’s built-in csv reader or pandas in chunks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Approach 1: Use the built-in csv reader, then build DataFrames as you go
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

import csv
import requests
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

def stream_csv_as_dataframe(url, chunk_size=8192, process_chunk=None):
    """
    Streams a remote CSV file in small chunks (chunk_size bytes at a time),
    converts each chunk of lines to a temporary DataFrame, and optionally
    processes it.

    :param url: The CSV URL to stream from.
    :param chunk_size: How many bytes to read at a time from the response.
    :param process_chunk: A callable that processes each DataFrame chunk 
                          (e.g. store it, filter, or accumulate).
    :return: None by default, but you could also accumulate results if needed.
    """
    response = requests.get(url, stream=True)
    response.raise_for_status()

    # Buffer to collect partial lines as they arrive
    buffer = []
    
    # We accumulate lines in "buffer", then parse them once we find 
    # complete line breaks
    for chunk in response.iter_content(chunk_size=chunk_size):
        # Decode the chunk from bytes to text
        text_chunk = chunk.decode('utf-8', errors='replace')
        # Split by newlines
        lines = text_chunk.split('\n')

        # The first line in "lines" extends the last partial line from buffer
        buffer[-1:] = [buffer[-1] + lines[0]] if buffer else [lines[0]]
        # Now the rest of the lines (except possibly the last one) are complete
        complete_lines = lines[1:-1]  # everything in between the first and last
        buffer.extend(complete_lines)
        
        # The final element of lines could be an incomplete line 
        # (i.e., chunk boundary in the middle of a CSV row)
        last_line = lines[-1]
        # If the chunk ended exactly on a newline, last_line is a complete line, 
        # otherwise we hold it in buffer for the next iteration
        if text_chunk[-1] == '\n':
            buffer.append(last_line)  # it's a complete line
            # Now parse everything in buffer
            data_frame = parse_lines_to_df(buffer)
            if process_chunk:
                process_chunk(data_frame)
            buffer = []  # reset after processing
        else:
            # Save last_line for the next chunk
            buffer.append(last_line)

    # After streaming ends, if anything is still in buffer, parse it:
    if buffer:
        data_frame = parse_lines_to_df(buffer)
        if process_chunk:
            process_chunk(data_frame)

def parse_lines_to_df(lines):
    """
    Given a list of CSV lines, parse them as a pandas DataFrame.
    Here we assume comma-separated, no header repeated in chunks, etc.
    Adjust to your real-world CSV format (headers, delimiters, etc.).
    """
    csv_buffer = StringIO("\n".join(lines))
    reader = csv.reader(csv_buffer, delimiter=',')
    rows = list(reader)

    if not rows:
        return pd.DataFrame()  # empty

    # If your CSV has a header in the very first chunk:
    # header = rows[0]
    # data = rows[1:]
    # If each chunk has no repeated header, you might store the header in an outer scope.
    # For simplicity, assume here that the first row is always the header:
    header = rows[0]
    data = rows[1:]
    df_chunk = pd.DataFrame(data, columns=header)
    return df_chunk

# Example usage:
# Define how each chunk’s DataFrame is processed/accumulated:
def process_chunk(df_chunk):
    print("Processing DataFrame chunk with shape:", df_chunk.shape)
    # do something: store, filter, transform, etc.

# stream_csv_as_dataframe("https://example.com/large.csv", process_chunk=process_chunk)


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Approach 2: Use pandas.read_csv directly with chunksize
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Pandas has a built-in “chunked” reading mechanism if you do not need to handle 
very complicated partial-line logic. In many cases, simply doing:

import pandas as pd

df_iter = pd.read_csv("https://example.com/large.csv", chunksize=10000)

for df_chunk in df_iter:
    # process df_chunk here

will stream data internally in chunks. Note that:
• It will not hold the entire dataset in memory at once.  
• Pandas does still need to read through all of the bytes from the HTTP response internally, but it does it lazily in chunks.  
• If your CSV is huge, keep an eye on memory usage; the chunk size might need to be tuned.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. The built-in csv approach (Approach 1) gives you the most control over how bytes arrive, how they are decoded, and how incomplete lines are handled at chunk boundaries.  
2. Pandas with chunksize (Approach 2) is far simpler but will handle most typical streaming CSV scenarios automatically.  
3. In both approaches, you never have to “fully download” the file to disk; you process it incrementally in-memory in chunks.

instruction: How to write a program in Python to calculate flight path
output:
Below is a simple example of how you could write a Python program to calculate the flight path of a projectile (often called a “ballistic flight path”). In this scenario, an object is launched with an initial speed and angle, and we plot its 2D path through the air under the influence of gravity. 

If you are looking for an aviation (airplane) flight path between two locations on Earth, see the notes at the end for additional suggestions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Projectile (Ballistic) Flight Path Example
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Key ideas:
• We assume no air resistance; only gravity acts on the projectile.  
• Initial speed V₀ and launch angle θ determine the trajectory.  
• The horizontal displacement (x) and vertical displacement (y) follow standard kinematic equations:
  
    x(t) = V₀*cos(θ)*t  
    y(t) = V₀*sin(θ)*t - (1/2)*g*t²  

(where g is the gravitational acceleration, typically 9.81 m/s²).

Below is a short Python script using NumPy and Matplotlib to compute and plot the trajectory.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Example Code
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

import math
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def projectile_flight_path(initial_speed, launch_angle_degrees, g=9.81):
    """
    Calculates the flight path of a projectile launched at a given speed 
    and angle (in degrees), ignoring air resistance.
    
    Args:
        initial_speed (float): Initial speed in m/s.
        launch_angle_degrees (float): Launch angle in degrees above the horizontal.
        g (float): Gravitational acceleration (m/s^2), default = 9.81.
    
    Returns:
        t_vals (np.ndarray): Times at which positions are calculated.
        x_vals (np.ndarray): Horizontal positions (m).
        y_vals (np.ndarray): Vertical positions (m).
    """
    # Convert angle to radians
    launch_angle_radians = math.radians(launch_angle_degrees)

    # Horizontal and vertical components of the initial velocity
    vx = initial_speed * math.cos(launch_angle_radians)
    vy = initial_speed * math.sin(launch_angle_radians)

    # Time of flight until the projectile lands back at y = 0
    # For a flat surface, total_time = (2 * vy) / g
    total_time = 2 * vy / g

    # Create a time array from t=0 to t=total_time
    t_vals = np.linspace(0, total_time, num=200)

    # Calculate x(t) and y(t) for each time
    x_vals = vx * t_vals
    y_vals = vy * t_vals - 0.5 * g * t_vals**2

    return t_vals, x_vals, y_vals

def main():
    # Define parameters
    speed = 50.0               # m/s
    angle = 45.0               # degrees
    gravity = 9.81             # m/s^2

    # Get the flight path
    t, x, y = projectile_flight_path(speed, angle, gravity)

    # Plot the path
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
    plt.plot(x, y, label=f"V0 = {speed} m/s, Angle = {angle}°")
    plt.title("Projectile Flight Path")
    plt.xlabel("Horizontal Distance (m)")
    plt.ylabel("Vertical Distance (m)")
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True)
    plt.show()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
How the Program Works
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Convert the launch angle from degrees to radians, because Python’s math functions use radians.  
2. Compute the initial velocity components along x and y (vx and vy).  
3. Compute total flight time using the formula for projectile motion on level ground: T = 2·vy / g.  
4. Generate a time array from 0 to T and compute (x, y) for each time step.  
5. Plot the results with matplotlib.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
If You Want an Airplane Flight Path:
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
• The “flight path” might refer to the great-circle route between two GPS coordinates. In that case, you can use geographic libraries such as geopy or pyproj.  
• For example, to compute distances between two airports based on latitude, longitude, and altitude, you might use:  
  from geopy.distance import great_circle  
  distance_km = great_circle((lat1, lon1), (lat2, lon2)).kilometers  
• For more advanced flight planning (including waypoints, wind, altitude changes), you would use algorithms that consider speed, headings, and possibly real-world data such as atmospheric models.

Feel free to adapt the above examples for your specific application—whether it’s a projectile flight path or an airplane route across the globe.

instruction: Provide python code to calculate pie infinitely
output:
Below is a Python example demonstrating how to iteratively approximate π using the (fast-converging) Chudnovsky algorithm with arbitrary precision via the built-in decimal module. Although you cannot literally compute “infinitely many” digits (since time and memory are finite), you can keep increasing the requested precision as large as you like—subject only to practical resource limits.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# chudnovsky_pi.py

import math
from decimal import Decimal, getcontext

def chudnovsky_pi(num_terms: int, precision: int) -> Decimal:
    """
    Approximates π using the Chudnovsky algorithm.

    :param num_terms:   Number of summation terms to use. 
                        More terms => higher accuracy, but slower.
    :param precision:   Number of significant digits of precision.
    :return:            Approximation of π as a Decimal.
    """
    getcontext().prec = precision  # Set the decimal precision

    # Constants used in the Chudnovsky formula
    # C = 426880 * sqrt(10005)
    # Each 'term' of the series is added to S, then 1 / (C/S) = π.
    C = Decimal(426880) * Decimal(10005).sqrt()

    # Initialize the sum for the series
    M = 1
    L = 13591409
    X = 1
    S = Decimal(L)  # Running sum
    K = 6  # The K multiplier starts at 6 and increases by 12 each iteration

    for i in range(1, num_terms):
        # M = M * (K^3 - 16K) / i^3
        M = (M * (K**3 - 16*K)) // (i**3)

        L += 545140134
        X *= -262537412640768000  #  (-1)^k * 640320^(3k*2)

        # Add the term to the series S:
        # term = (M * L) / X
        term = Decimal(M * L) / Decimal(X)
        S += term

        K += 12

    # π = C / S
    return C / S

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Example of computing Pi iteratively and printing partial approximations
    
    # How many digits of precision we want at the start
    initial_precision = 50
    
    # For demonstration, we will approximate pi multiple times, increasing the terms each time
    # In principle, you can continue indefinitely, constrained by time and memory.
    for terms in [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50]:
        pi_approx = chudnovsky_pi(num_terms=terms, precision=initial_precision)
        print(f"Using {terms} terms => {pi_approx}")
    
    # If you want to keep going "forever", you could do something like:
    # (Be cautious: computing very large numbers of digits can be slow.)
    #
    # import itertools
    # terms = 0
    # while True:
    #     terms += 1
    #     pi_approx = chudnovsky_pi(num_terms=terms, precision=initial_precision)
    #     print(f"Iteration {terms}, pi ~ {pi_approx}")
    #
    #     # Optionally increase precision if desired:
    #     initial_precision += 2  # increase precision slightly after each iteration
    #
    #     # Sleep or break conditions can be applied to avoid infinite looping.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation of key parts:

1. decimal.getcontext().prec:  
   Controls how many significant decimal digits the module will maintain. Increase this to compute more digits of π.

2. Chudnovsky Algorithm:  
   A very efficient series for π that converges quickly. The general formula is:  
       1 / π = 12 * ∑ ( (-1)^k * (6k)! * (13591409 + 545140134k) ) / ( (3k)! * (k!)^3 * 640320^(3k + 1.5) )  

   In code, we transform constants and reuse intermediate results (factorials, powers) iteratively to avoid recomputing big factorials from scratch each step.

3. Infinite/Long-Running Loop:  
   You can wrap the procedure in a while True loop to keep refining π. Just be mindful of practical limitations such as runtime and memory.

This approach gives you a way to continually approximate π to arbitrarily high precision—effectively getting “closer and closer infinitely,” as allowed by your computational resources.
