instruction:
You're an expert triathlon coach using the latest science-based training methodologies. Please write me a training plan for my first Ironman 70.3 on the 2nd of June that starts in January. The training plan should include all three disciplines and be tailored to my specific experience level: I have no previous swimming experience, I have a solid foundation in cycling and I am an experienced runner. Build the plan in a way that allows me to improve my existing level of fitness in running while building enough fitness in the other two disciplines to finish the half ironman in June. 
I want to train 6 days a week but work a full time job, so keep in mind that I can do longer sessions only on the weekends.
output:
Below is a structured, science-informed training plan designed to take you from January through to your first Ironman 70.3 on June 2. It’s built around six training days per week, with shorter weekday sessions (to accommodate your work schedule) and longer sessions on the weekend. It also accounts for your strong running background, your solid cycling base, and your lack of swim experience.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PLAN OVERVIEW
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Total Duration: ~20 Weeks (January 1 → Race Day: June 2)  
• Training Phases:  
  1) Base (Weeks 1–6)  
  2) Build (Weeks 7–12)  
  3) Peak (Weeks 13–18)  
  4) Taper (Weeks 19–20)  

You’ll train six days each week, with one rest day. A typical structure might be:
• Mon – Swim (technique-focused) + Optional short run (if time)  
• Tue – Run (intervals or tempo)  
• Wed – Bike (moderate to hard)  
• Thu – Swim (endurance-focused) + Easy run or brick session  
• Fri – Rest or short active recovery (light yoga, mobility, or easy spin)  
• Sat – Long bike or bike-run brick  
• Sun – Long run  

Note: Feel free to swap days around depending on your schedule, but maintain the logic—shorter, more focused weekday sessions; longer weekend sessions.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PHASE 1: BASE (Weeks 1–6, January to Mid-February)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Goals:
• Develop basic swim technique and confidence in the water.  
• Maintain and gently build cycling and running fitness without overloading.  
• Establish consistent training habits (6 sessions/week).  

Focus Points:
• Swimming: Emphasize technique and drills. Consider hiring a swim coach for a few sessions or find a masters swim group if possible.  
• Cycling: Keep it moderate; focus on endurance (Zone 2 to low Zone 3).  
• Running: Maintain your base with one moderate-long run on the weekend; incorporate easy runs to avoid injury.  

Example Weekly Structure (Base Phase):
• Monday (Swim + Optional Short Run)  
  – Swim: 30–45 min. Warm-up with drills (catch-up drill, single-arm drill). Focus on proper breathing and body alignment.  
  – Short Run (Optional): 20–30 min easy (Zone 1–2) if time allows.  

• Tuesday (Run – Intervals or Tempo)  
  – Run: 45–60 min. After a warm-up, do short tempo intervals or hill repeats (e.g., 4–6 × 2 min at 10K effort/hill repeats). Cool down properly.  

• Wednesday (Bike – Moderate)  
  – Cycling: 60–75 min on a trainer or outside. Keep intensity in Zone 2–3. Focus on smooth pedaling and staying steadily aerobic.  

• Thursday (Swim + Easy Run)  
  – Swim: 30–45 min. Emphasis on breathing rhythm, body rotation, and some short endurance sets like 4 × 100m with 30 seconds rest.  
  – Easy Run: 20–30 min (Zone 1–2) if time allows.  

• Friday (Rest or Active Recovery)  
  – Rest: Complete day off, or do light mobility/yoga. This is especially important to allow muscles to recover.  

• Saturday (Long Bike)  
  – Cycling: 1.5–2 hours. Keep most of it in Zone 2, focusing on aerobic capacity. End with a few 1-minute faster efforts if you feel good.  

• Sunday (Long Run)  
  – Run: 45–60 min. Keep it easy to moderate. Gradually progress to 75 min as the weeks go by if you feel comfortable.  

At the end of Week 3 and Week 6, reduce volume by ~20% (especially intensity) to let your body absorb the training load.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PHASE 2: BUILD (Weeks 7–12, Mid-February to End of March)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Goals:
• Increase aerobic endurance and overall volume in all disciplines.  
• Begin including more structured speed/interval sessions in bike and run.  
• Increase swim endurance (continuous swims up to 800–1000m).  

Focus Points:
• Swimming: Shift focus from just drills to building distance (e.g., 400- to 800m continuous swims). Maintain technique drills in warm-up.  
• Cycling: Incorporate more threshold or sweet spot intervals mid-week, keep the long ride on weekends.  
• Running: Maintain at least one tempo/interval session per week + one long run.  

Example Weekly Structure (Build Phase):
• Monday (Swim – Technique + Endurance)  
  – Swim: 45–60 min. (e.g., 200m warm-up + drills, then 4–6 × 100m at steady pace with 20–30 sec rest, cooldown).  

• Tuesday (Run – Tempo)  
  – Run: 60 min total. After a warm-up, do a 20 min tempo block at half-marathon pace, then cool down.  

• Wednesday (Bike – Threshold/Intervals)  
  – Cycling: 60–90 min. Could include 2–3 × 8–12 min at sweet spot or threshold (Zone 3–4) with equal recovery.  

• Thursday (Swim + Easy Run)  
  – Swim: 45–60 min. Similar set structure: 6–8 × 100m or 3–4 × 200m with moderate effort.  
  – Easy Run: 30 min at conversational pace.  

• Friday (Rest or Short Active Recovery)  
  – Optional: Light spin (< 45 min) or mobility/yoga if you feel overly fatigued. Otherwise full rest.  

• Saturday (Long Bike or Brick)  
  – Cycling: 2–3 hours, mostly Zone 2 with a few efforts in Zone 3.  
  – Optional Brick: Transition immediately to a 20–30 min easy run to get used to running off the bike.  

• Sunday (Long Run)  
  – Run: 60–90 min, starting easy, building to steady pace in the last 20 minutes.  

By the end of this phase, you should be comfortable swimming continuous 800m sets, riding 2–3 hours steadily, and running up to 90 minutes on Sundays. Every third or fourth week, scale back by ~20% to promote recovery.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PHASE 3: PEAK (Weeks 13–18, April to Mid-May)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Goals:
• Push swimming volume closer to race distance (1900m) through structured interval sets and a growing continuous swim.  
• Increase the long bike to 3–4 hours.  
• Maintain or increase the long run up to ~1 hr 45 min (if comfortable) while including some race-pace intervals.  

Focus Points:
• Swimming: Introduce 1500–2000m workouts, including sets like 3 × 400m or 1 × 1000m + 1 × 500m. Consider practicing open-water skills if possible.  
• Cycling: Add race-pace (Zone 2–3) intervals in your long ride, and keep a short but intense mid-week session.  
• Running: One interval or tempo session mid-week, plus a progressive long run on Sunday.  

Example Weekly Structure (Peak Phase):
• Monday (Swim – Longer Sets)  
  – Swim: 60 min. 200m warm-up + drills, main set: 3 × 400m (Zone 2–3) with 1 min rest, cooldown.  

• Tuesday (Run – Interval/Tempo)  
  – Run: 60–75 min. Example: 4–6 × 5 min at 10K pace with 90 sec jog recovery.  

• Wednesday (Bike – Threshold or VO2)  
  – Cycling: 60–90 min with 2–3 × 10 min at threshold (Zone 4) or 4–5 × 3 min VO2 (Zone 5) with full recovery.  

• Thursday (Swim + Easy Run or Brick)  
  – Swim: 45–60 min. Focus on shorter repeats (100–200m) working on speed and form.  
  – Easy Run/Brick: 30 min easy OR quick 15–20 min run off a short bike.  

• Friday (Rest or Active Recovery)  
  – Light yoga or stretching session.  

• Saturday (Long Bike or Brick)  
  – Cycling: 3–4 hours. Include segments at half-Iron pace (Zone 2–3).  
  – Brick Run: 20–30 min at an easy, relaxed pace.  

• Sunday (Long Run)  
  – Run: 90–105 min. In the latter weeks, consider 2–3 × 15–20 min at planned race intensity near the end of the run.  

During the Peak Phase, you should complete at least a few brick sessions that closely mimic race day effort to practice pacing and nutrition strategies.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PHASE 4: TAPER (Weeks 19–20, Late May to Race Day)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Goals:
• Sharpen fitness and arrive at the start line fresh and injury-free.  
• Reduce volume by ~30–50% while maintaining some intensity.  

Focus Points:
• Swimming: 1–2 sessions per week of shorter, crisp intervals (e.g., 6 × 100m).  
• Cycling: Two shorter rides including a few race-pace efforts, and one moderate ride on the weekend (no more than 2 hours two weeks out, then 1–1.5 hours one week out).  
• Running: One short tempo/interval run early in Week 19, but reduce volume to about 50% of peak by the week of the race.  

Example Weekly Structure (Taper Phase):
• Week 19:  
  – Keep 2 swims but reduce volume. Shorter interval sets (like 6 × 100m).  
  – One mid-week bike with a few short Zone 3 bursts, plus one weekend ride ~1.5–2 hours easy/moderate.  
  – One mid-week run with tempo intervals (like 3 × 5 min), plus an easy weekend run of 45–60 min.  

• Week 20 (Race Week):  
  – 1–2 short swims (20–30 min) at easy/moderate effort.  
  – 1–2 short bikes with a couple of 2–3 min race-pace efforts.  
  – 1 short run early in the week (30–40 min) with a few strides.  
  – Allow 1–2 days completely off or super easy (mobility, stretching).  

RACE DAY (June 2):
• Wake up early, eat a familiar, easily digested breakfast.  
• Hydrate properly but don’t overdo it.  
• Rehearse your transitions mentally.  
• Execute your plan: stay steady in the swim, maintain controlled effort on the bike, and pace your run to finish strong.  

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ADDITIONAL TIPS & CONSIDERATIONS
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Swim Lessons/Coaching: With no prior swimming experience, consider technique-focused lessons early on. Form matters more than volume for improvement and injury prevention.  
2. Recovery & Sleep: With a full-time job, prioritize sleep (7–8 hours) and nutrition (protein-rich, balanced diet) to support recovery.  
3. Strength Training (Optional if Time Permits): Light core and strength work (1–2 sessions/week) can help injury-proof you and improve performance. Focus on functional movements like planks, glute bridges, lunges, and light upper-body exercises for swimming.  
4. Listen to Your Body: Adjust volume or intensity if you’re overly fatigued or notice injury warning signs. Consistency is key—avoid big spikes in training load.  
5. Periodic Testing: Every ~6–8 weeks, do a time trial in each discipline (e.g., 400m or 1000m swim TT, 20-min bike FTP test, 5K or 10K run TT) to track progress and adjust pacing zones.  

By following this plan, gradually progressing your swim, bike, and run, and prioritizing recovery, you’ll be well-prepared to cross the finish line of your Ironman 70.3 in June. Best of luck, and enjoy the journey!

instruction: A package delivery Service will charge 3€ for shipping packages where the sum of the shortest and the longest side of the package must be below 50cm. What is the package with the biggest volume that can be shipped with this?
output:
A concise way to see why there is (effectively) a single “best” box is as follows.  Label the sides of the rectangular box by x ≤ y ≤ z.  The shipping rule says x + z < 50.  We want to maximize the volume V = x·y·z under these conditions.

■ First, note that there is no upper bound given on y in the problem statement, so to maximize volume one would make y as large as allowed.  Since y cannot exceed z (because y ≤ z), the largest possible choice is y = z.

■ Hence we reduce the problem to maximizing  
   V = x · z · z = xz²  
subject to x + z < 50 and x ≤ z.  We may regard x + z = 50 as the “limiting boundary” (we will approach it from below).

■ Because x ≤ z and x + z = 50, we must have x ≤ 25 and correspondingly z ≥ 25.  In fact we can rewrite z = 50 − x; then
   V(x) = x(50 − x)² = x(2500 − 100x + x²).
Taking the derivative and setting it to zero shows the unique positive critical point occurs at  
   x = 50/3 ≈ 16.67,     z = 100/3 ≈ 33.33.

■ At that point, one chooses y = z ≈ 33.33.  This yields
   Vmax ≈  (50/3)·(100/3)² = 500000/27 ≈ 18 518 cm³.

Strictly speaking, the constraint says x + z must be below 50 (not equal), so one cannot use exactly x = 50/3 and z = 100/3.  However, one can make x + z arbitrarily close to 50 from below, making the maximum volume arbitrarily close to 18 518 cm³.  In practical terms, the “best” dimensions are about  
   x ≈ 16.67 cm,   y ≈ 33.33 cm,   z ≈ 33.33 cm,  
giving the largest possible volume under the rule x + z < 50.

instruction: Please write a Python function that receives a data frame with columns date and winner and returns the longest number of consecutive win by Alice
output:
Below is a simple Python function that, given a pandas DataFrame with columns "date" and "winner", will return the longest streak (maximum number of consecutive wins) by Alice. The function first sorts the data by date (to ensure chronological order), then counts consecutive occurrences of “Alice,” and keeps track of the maximum streak:

import pandas as pd

def longest_alice_streak(df: pd.DataFrame) -> int:
    """
    Given a DataFrame with columns 'date' and 'winner',
    return the longest streak (number of consecutive wins) by Alice.
    """

    # Ensure the DataFrame is sorted by date
    df = df.sort_values(by="date")

    longest_streak = 0
    current_streak = 0

    for winner in df["winner"]:
        if winner == "Alice":
            current_streak += 1
            longest_streak = max(longest_streak, current_streak)
        else:
            current_streak = 0

    return longest_streak

Example usage:
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'date': ['2023-01-01', '2023-01-02', '2023-01-03', '2023-01-04', '2023-01-05'],
    'winner': ['Alice', 'Alice', 'Bob', 'Alice', 'Alice']
})

result = longest_alice_streak(df)
print(result)  # Outputs the longest streak of wins by Alice.

instruction: Can you generate an A level exam question on circular motion, with an according mark scheme and answer.
output:
Below is a sample A‑level Physics question on circular motion, including the question itself, a structured mark scheme, and a full worked answer.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
QUESTION
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
1) A small bead of mass m is attached to one end of a light, inextensible string of length L. The other end of the string is fixed to a point O on the ceiling. The bead is set into uniform circular motion in a horizontal plane such that the string makes a constant angle θ with the vertical.

   a) Sketch a clear force diagram showing all the forces acting on the bead and the geometry of the motion.  
   b) Show that the tension T in the string can be split into two components T cos θ and T sin θ, and hence write equations for:  
      i) The vertical balance of forces,  
      ii) The centripetal force causing the horizontal circular motion.  
   c) Derive an expression for the speed v of the bead in terms of g, L, and θ.  
   d) State what happens to the angle θ if the bead is made to rotate faster (briefly justify your answer).

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
MARK SCHEME
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Below is a suggested mark distribution and the key ideas or steps required for full credit. (Exact mark allocations may vary depending on the exam board’s conventions.)

(a) Sketch of forces (2 marks total)  
   • (1 mark) Correctly labeling weight mg acting vertically downward.  
   • (1 mark) Correctly labeling tension T in the string acting along the string, and indicating the horizontal circular path.

(b) Force components and equations (4 marks total)  
   i) Vertical balance (2 marks):  
      • (1 mark) Correctly stating that the vertical component of tension, T cos θ, balances mg.  
      • (1 mark) Correctly writing the equation T cos θ = mg.  

   ii) Horizontal (centripetal) component (2 marks):  
      • (1 mark) Correctly stating that T sin θ provides the centripetal force.  
      • (1 mark) Correctly writing the centripetal force equation T sin θ = m v² / r.  
        (Note: r is the radius of the horizontal circle; for a string of length L at angle θ, r = L sin θ.)

(c) Expression for v (4 marks total)  
   • (1 mark) Recognizing from T cos θ = mg that T = mg / cos θ.  
   • (1 mark) Substituting T into T sin θ = m v² / r.  
   • (1 mark) Using r = L sin θ, leading to mg / cos θ × sin θ = m v² / (L sin θ).  
   • (1 mark) Correct final expression: v = √(g L tan θ).  

(d) Effect of increasing rotation speed (2 marks total)  
   • (1 mark) Stating that, as speed increases, the horizontal component of tension must increase.  
   • (1 mark) Concluding that this requires a larger angle θ with the vertical (i.e., the string tilts further from the vertical as speed increases).

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
FULL WORKED ANSWER
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

(a) Force diagram:  
• The bead of mass m experiences two main forces:  
  1. Its weight mg, acting vertically downwards from its center of mass.  
  2. The tension T in the string, acting along the string towards the fixed point O.  
• The bead moves in a horizontal circular path of radius r, which is related to the string length by r = L sin θ.

(b) Force components and equations:  
   i) Vertical balance: Since the bead does not accelerate vertically, the vertical component of the tension must balance the weight:  
      T cos θ = mg.  

   ii) Horizontal (centripetal) force: The horizontal component of tension provides the centripetal force that keeps the bead moving in a circle at constant speed v:  
      T sin θ = m (v² / r).  

(c) Determining the speed v:  
• From T cos θ = mg, we have T = mg / cos θ.  
• Substituting T into T sin θ = m (v² / r):  
  (mg / cos θ) × sin θ = m v² / r.  
• Simplify the left side: mg (sin θ / cos θ) = mg tan θ.  
• Hence, mg tan θ = m v² / r.  
• Note that r = L sin θ. Substituting r:  
  mg tan θ = m v² / (L sin θ).  
• Cancel m on both sides and rearrange for v²:  
  g tan θ = v² / (L sin θ)  
  ⇒ v² = g L sin θ tan θ = g L tan θ sin θ.  
• Recognizing tan θ = (sin θ / cos θ), we get:  
  v² = g L (sin² θ / cos θ).  
• Alternatively, we can simplify directly to the more common form:  
  v = √(g L tan θ).  

  (Both expressions are correct; exam boards often present v = √(g L tan θ) as the typical final form.)

(d) Effect of increasing speed on θ:  
• If the bead is made to rotate faster, a larger centripetal force is needed.  
• Since T sin θ = m v² / r must increase, and T cos θ = mg remains the same unless speed changes dramatically, one way to increase the horizontal component T sin θ is to increase θ.  
• Therefore, as speed increases, θ increases (the string tilts further from the vertical).

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

This question and solution set address key aspects of uniform circular motion in a conical pendulum context, aligning well with typical A‑level Physics requirements.

instruction: Tell me the highest yield 15 facts to help me study for the nuclear cardiology board exam I have to take tomorrow. Focus on providing me with info that is likely to be on the test, but is more obscure than super common information.
output:
Below are 15 higher-yield but somewhat “less-discussed” facts that could show up on a nuclear cardiology board exam. These can be easy to overlook, yet they are important details where questions often arise.

1) Low-Level Exercise in Vasodilator Stress  
   • When patients undergo vasodilator stress, adding a very low-level exercise (e.g., slow walking on a treadmill) can reduce liver/bowel uptake of tracer and improve image quality.  
   • This approach often results in fewer artifacts and clearer delineation of inferior wall perfusion.  

2) Rubidium-82 PET: Unusual Half-Life and Generator  
   • Rubidium-82 has a very short half-life of about 75 seconds. It is eluted from a Strontium-82/Rubidium-82 generator, which must be replaced approximately every 4–6 weeks.  
   • The short half-life allows rapid sequential imaging, but also demands precise attention to timing and logistics in a PET lab setting.  

3) LBBB and Coronary-Artery Disease (CAD) Perfusion Patterns  
   • Left bundle branch block often causes a false-positive, septal “defect” or is associated with diminished uptake in the septum during exercise or vasodilator stress.  
   • Pharmacologic stress with Dobutamine (instead of vasodilators) can help reduce false-positive reversible defects in patients with LBBB since dobutamine doesn’t rely on coronary vasodilation to the same extent.

4) SSS, SRS, SDS: Summed Stress, Rest, and Difference Scores  
   • The Summed Stress Score (SSS), Summed Rest Score (SRS), and Summed Difference Score (SDS = SSS – SRS) provide a quantitative measure of perfusion abnormality.  
   • An SDS ≥ 2 often indicates a true perfusion defect; higher numbers correlate with increasing severity of ischemia and/or scar.

5) Ventricular Cavity Dilatation on Stress Imaging (TID Ratio)  
   • TID (Transient Ischemic Dilation) is considered present if the stress-to-rest cavity size ratio exceeds a certain threshold (commonly ≥ 1.19 or so for 99mTc-based agents).  
   • TID on myocardial perfusion imaging can be a marker of extensive ischemia or multi-vessel disease, even if perfusion appears otherwise normal.  

6) Attenuation Artifacts vs. True Defect  
   • Breast tissue and diaphragmatic attenuation can mimic inferior or anterolateral wall defects.  
   • Use of attenuation correction (via CT-based methods) helps differentiate soft-tissue artifact from true myocardial hypoperfusion.

7) Reverse Redistribution in 201Tl Imaging  
   • Reverse redistribution refers to a phenomenon in thallium scans where initially normal or near-normal areas appear to worsen (diminished tracer uptake) on delayed images.  
   • This pattern can be seen in viable myocardium with stunned or hibernating tissue that demonstrates delayed tracer washout or altered uptake kinetics.

8) MUGA (Multigated Acquisition) Scans and EF  
   • MUGA scans (also called radionuclide ventriculography, RNV) measure left ventricular ejection fraction with high reproducibility.  
   • Slight differences in gating (e.g., arrhythmias, irregular R-R intervals) can affect EF calculations. Ensuring stable rhythm/gating is crucial.  

9) Key Differences Between 99mTc-Sestamibi and 99mTc-Tetrofosmin  
   • Both labeled compounds are used for myocardial perfusion SPECT, but 99mTc-tetrofosmin has slightly faster liver clearance, often resulting in fewer subdiaphragmatic attenuation artifacts.  
   • 99mTc-sestamibi has a higher first-pass extraction but can have greater hepatic uptake, sometimes complicating inferior wall imaging early post-injection.

10) Coronary Flow Reserve Assessment on PET  
   • PET tracers such as 13N-ammonia, 82Rb, or 15O-water can measure absolute myocardial blood flow in mL/min/g and calculate coronary flow reserve (stress flow ÷ rest flow).  
   • A flow reserve < 2.0 (some use 2.5 as a common benchmark) suggests significant coronary microvascular dysfunction or epicardial disease.

11) Regadenoson vs. Adenosine/Dipyridamole  
   • Regadenoson (Lexiscan) is a selective A2A receptor agonist with fewer side effects and a longer half-life than adenosine.  
   • It is given as a fixed dose (commonly 0.4 mg in 5 mL) and does not require weight-based dosing or continuous infusion; this simplicity is a major benefit clinically.

12) PYP Imaging for Cardiac Amyloid  
   • 99mTc-Pyrophosphate (PYP) imaging can differentiate transthyretin (TTR) amyloid (ATTR) from light chain (AL) amyloid in some patients with suspected cardiac amyloidosis.  
   • High-grade PYP uptake (≥ Grade 2 or with a heart-to-contralateral lung ratio of ≥ 1.5) is typically associated with ATTR rather than AL.

13) Obesity and Supine vs. Prone Imaging  
   • Prone imaging can help minimize diaphragmatic or breast attenuation, especially in obese patients.  
   • However, prone imaging may introduce small apparent lateral or inferior perfusion changes. Familiarity with typical positional artifacts helps avoid misinterpretation.

14) Gated SPECT and Tidal Volume/Respiration  
   • Marked respiratory motion during SPECT acquisitions can degrade images and create pseudo-defects.  
   • Newer cameras or software that correct for motion can significantly reduce artifact, but examiners may ask about the pitfalls of motion-correction (e.g., incorrectly matching raw data or introducing blurring).

15) Stunned Myocardium vs. Hibernating Myocardium  
   • Stunned myocardium is temporarily dysfunctional after reperfusion but is perfused normally and often takes days to weeks to recover.  
   • Hibernating myocardium is chronically underperfused, with persistent contractile dysfunction that may improve after revascularization. Viability imaging (e.g., 18F-FDG PET, 201Tl redistribution) can distinguish between scar and hibernation.

These points often appear in study materials yet can be overshadowed by more basic topics (like standard artifacts or test protocols). Reviewing these nuanced details should give you an extra edge on your exam. Good luck in your preparation!

instruction: count distinct values in a column given a constraint from another column using over clause in ssms
output:
In SQL Server versions prior to 2022, there is no direct syntax for COUNT(DISTINCT …) OVER (PARTITION BY …). If you try something like:

  COUNT(DISTINCT SomeColumn) OVER (PARTITION BY AnotherColumn)

you will get an error. In SQL Server 2022 (or in Azure SQL Database), this syntax is allowed. For older versions, you have to work around it. Below are two common approaches.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Using a SUBQUERY or CROSS APPLY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

If your goal is simply to list, for each row, how many distinct values occur in SomeColumn for that row’s partition (based on AnotherColumn), you can use a subquery or a CROSS APPLY. For example:

SELECT 
    t.SomeKey,
    t.AnotherColumn,
    t.SomeColumn,
    DistinctCount = (
        SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT t2.SomeColumn)
        FROM YourTable t2
        WHERE t2.AnotherColumn = t.AnotherColumn
    )
FROM YourTable t;

This approach is often straightforward but can be slower on large tables if you do not have proper indexing.

Alternatively, you can use CROSS APPLY, which may help performance if you filter rows in the outer query:

SELECT
    t.SomeKey,
    t.AnotherColumn,
    t.SomeColumn,
    x.DistinctCount
FROM YourTable t
CROSS APPLY
(
    SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT t2.SomeColumn) AS DistinctCount
    FROM YourTable t2
    WHERE t2.AnotherColumn = t.AnotherColumn
) x;

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) Using a WINDOW FUNCTION WORKAROUND (ROW_NUMBER or DENSE_RANK Trick)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Because COUNT(DISTINCT …) OVER (PARTITION BY …) is not supported before SQL Server 2022, a common workaround is:

• Identify the “first occurrence” (or “unique occurrence”) of SomeColumn within each partition.
• Sum those unique occurrences as 1 each.

For example, you can use ROW_NUMBER() over (PARTITION BY AnotherColumn, SomeColumn) to label duplicates, then sum up the first-row flags:

WITH CTE AS
(
    SELECT
        t.*,
        rn = ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY t.AnotherColumn, t.SomeColumn
                                 ORDER BY (SELECT NULL))
    FROM YourTable t
)
SELECT
    SomeKey,
    AnotherColumn,
    SomeColumn,
    -- Count distinct SomeColumn in each partition by summing “first occurrence” only
    DISTINCT_Count = SUM(CASE WHEN rn = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
                      OVER (PARTITION BY AnotherColumn)
FROM CTE;

Explanation of the CTE approach:

1) In the CTE, we generate rn = 1 for the first occurrence of (AnotherColumn, SomeColumn).  
2) For duplicate occurrences of (AnotherColumn, SomeColumn), rn will be 2, 3, etc.  
3) Back in the main SELECT, we use a window function SUM(CASE WHEN rn=1 THEN 1 END) OVER (PARTITION BY AnotherColumn).  
   • This effectively counts how many unique (SomeColumn) values exist for each AnotherColumn partition.

That way, each row in the result shows the total distinct count for its partition.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3) SQL Server 2022 Syntax
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Starting in SQL Server 2022 (and in Azure SQL Database), you can finally write:

SELECT
    t.*,
    COUNT(DISTINCT SomeColumn) OVER (PARTITION BY AnotherColumn) AS DistinctCount
FROM YourTable t;

Keep in mind this requires SQL Server 2022 or higher.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

• For older SQL Server versions, emulate COUNT(DISTINCT …) in window functions by using a subquery, a CROSS APPLY, or a row-numbering trick (ROW_NUMBER or DENSE_RANK).  
• For SQL Server 2022 or Azure SQL Database, you can directly use COUNT(DISTINCT …) OVER (PARTITION BY …) as intended.

instruction: Hi, I would like the python code for turning excel cells into coloured powerpoint squares
output:
Below is a starter Python script showing how you can read cell-fill colors from an Excel file (using openpyxl) and then create corresponding colored rectangles in a PowerPoint file (using python-pptx). This example:

• Reads an Excel file named "example.xlsx."  
• Takes the active worksheet’s first 5 rows and 5 columns (adjust to suit).  
• Creates a new PowerPoint presentation.  
• On a blank slide, it draws rectangles whose fill colors match the corresponding Excel cell’s fill color.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Required installs (via pip):
#   pip install openpyxl
#   pip install python-pptx

from openpyxl import load_workbook
from pptx import Presentation
from pptx.util import Inches
from pptx.dml.color import RGBColor
from pptx.enum.shapes import MSO_SHAPE

def excel_cells_to_ppt_squares(
    excel_file='example.xlsx', 
    ppt_file='colored_squares.pptx',
    rows=5, 
    cols=5
):
    # Load workbook and select active sheet
    workbook = load_workbook(excel_file)
    sheet = workbook.active
    
    # Create a new PowerPoint Presentation and add a blank slide
    prs = Presentation()
    blank_slide_layout = prs.slide_layouts[6]  # index 6 is usually a blank layout
    slide = prs.slides.add_slide(blank_slide_layout)
    
    # Define the top-left position for drawing squares (inches)
    top_start = Inches(1)
    left_start = Inches(1)
    
    # Define the size of each square
    square_width = Inches(0.5)
    square_height = Inches(0.5)
    
    for row_idx, row in enumerate(sheet.iter_rows(min_row=1, max_row=rows, min_col=1, max_col=cols), start=0):
        for col_idx, cell in enumerate(row, start=0):
            
            # Attempt to retrieve fill color (in Excel, the fill color is often in "start_color" or "fgColor")
            fill_color = cell.fill.start_color.rgb  # e.g., 'FF00FF00' for pure green
            
            # If the cell does not have an explicit fill, or it's 'FFFFFFFF' (white), handle fallback
            if fill_color is None or fill_color == '00000000' or fill_color == 'FFFFFFFF':
                # Example fallback to white or skip making shapes
                fill_color = 'FFFFFFFF'  # fallback to white
                
            # PowerPoint needs the RGB as three hex bytes; fill_color is typically 8 hex chars like "FFRRGGBB"
            # so we need to extract the RRGGBB part
            # fill_color[0:2] is the "Alpha channel" (usually 'FF'), fill_color[2:4] is R, [4:6] G, [6:8] B
            red_hex   = fill_color[2:4]
            green_hex = fill_color[4:6]
            blue_hex  = fill_color[6:8]
            
            # Convert the hex strings (e.g., 'FF') to integers
            r = int(red_hex, 16)
            g = int(green_hex, 16)
            b = int(blue_hex, 16)
            
            # Calculate the position of the square in the slide
            left = left_start + Inches(col_idx * 0.6)  # slightly spaced horizontally
            top  = top_start  + Inches(row_idx * 0.6)  # slightly spaced vertically
            
            # Add a rectangle shape to the slide
            shape = slide.shapes.add_shape(
                MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, 
                left, top, 
                square_width, 
                square_height
            )
            
            # Fill the shape with the color
            shape.fill.solid()
            shape.fill.fore_color.rgb = RGBColor(r, g, b)
            
            # Optionally remove outline
            shape.line.fill.background()
    
    # Save the resulting presentation
    prs.save(ppt_file)
    print(f"PowerPoint saved as '{ppt_file}'.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    excel_cells_to_ppt_squares(
        excel_file="example.xlsx",
        ppt_file="colored_squares.pptx",
        rows=5,
        cols=5
    )

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Adjust the code to:  
• Cover the exact rows/columns you want from Excel.  
• Tweak positioning and sizing of the rectangles to match your preferred layout.  
• Provide a fallback color for cells that do not have an explicit fill.

instruction: Query an excel table using MySQL to select dram excel table tree species by diameter class, count the number of representation of the diameter class and some volume of the total
output:
Below is an example of how you might structure a MySQL query to group tree data (from a table originally imported from Excel) by diameter classes, count how many records fall into each class, and sum a volume column. 

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Import your Excel file into MySQL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

   You can’t directly query an .xlsx file in MySQL. To query your Excel data:
   • Convert the Excel file to CSV.
   • Use MySQL’s LOAD DATA INFILE or a GUI tool (e.g., MySQL Workbench) to import the CSV into a MySQL table—say it’s called dram_data.

   Assume the final MySQL table dram_data has columns:
     • id (optional primary key)
     • species (text)
     • diameter (numeric)
     • volume (numeric)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) Choose or define diameter classes
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

   For example, you might want diameter classes in 10-cm increments:
     • 0–9.9  
     • 10–19.9  
     • 20–29.9  
     • etc.

   You can implement these classes in SQL using a CASE statement or a mathematical expression. Below are two common approaches.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3A) Using a CASE statement
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

   The CASE approach is more explicit and allows you to label classes exactly as you wish:

   SELECT 
       species,
       CASE 
         WHEN diameter < 10 THEN '0–9.9' 
         WHEN diameter >= 10 AND diameter < 20 THEN '10–19.9'
         WHEN diameter >= 20 AND diameter < 30 THEN '20–29.9'
         WHEN diameter >= 30 AND diameter < 40 THEN '30–39.9'
         ELSE '40+'
       END AS diameter_class,
       COUNT(*) AS count_trees,
       SUM(volume) AS total_volume
   FROM dram_data
   GROUP BY species, diameter_class
   ORDER BY species, diameter_class;

   Explanation:
   • CASE … END: Categorizes diameter into labeled bins.  
   • COUNT(*): Counts how many rows fall in each diameter_class per species.  
   • SUM(volume): Adds up volume in each diameter_class per species.  
   • GROUP BY species, diameter_class: Groups records by both species and the newly defined diameter_class.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3B) Using integer math to bin diameters automatically
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

   If you prefer to programmatically define classes in fixed increments (say 10 cm), you can group by integer division or truncation:

   SELECT 
       species,
       CONCAT(
         TRUNCATE(diameter/10, 0)*10,
         '–',
         TRUNCATE(diameter/10, 0)*10 + 9.9
       ) AS diameter_class,
       COUNT(*) AS count_trees,
       SUM(volume) AS total_volume
   FROM dram_data
   GROUP BY species,
       TRUNCATE(diameter/10, 0)  -- bin index
   ORDER BY species, TRUNCATE(diameter/10, 0);

   Explanation:
   • TRUNCATE(diameter/10, 0): Divides the diameter by 10 and removes the decimal, effectively creating bins of size 10. For example, diameters 10–19.9 become 1 in integer form, 20–29.9 become 2, etc.  
   • CONCAT(...): Builds a text string (e.g., “10–19.9”) for readability.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4) Insights from the query
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   From the query results, for each species and diameter_class, you will see:
   • How many trees fall into that diameter class (count_trees).  
   • The total volume contributed by trees in that class (total_volume).  

Adjust column names, table names, or diameter bin widths according to how your actual data is structured. Once set up correctly, you’ll get a grouped summary by diameter classes for each tree species in your MySQL table derived from your original Excel data.

instruction: Help me filter and delete each row in an excel table, where value of a certain column is 0
output:
Below are two common approaches to remove all rows that have a value of 0 in a specific column. The first approach uses Excel’s built-in Filter feature (no programming required), and the second approach uses a small VBA macro.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Using Excel’s Filter Feature (No VBA)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Open your worksheet and select your table (or the entire range).  
2. On the “Data” tab in the ribbon, click the “Filter” button.  
   – You should now see drop-down arrows appear on each column header.  
3. Click the drop-down arrow for the column you want to check for zero.  
4. From the filter options, uncheck all values, then check only “0.”  
   – This will show only the rows where that column’s value is zero.  
5. Select all visible rows (you can click and drag, or press Ctrl+A if your entire set of rows is only the filtered list).  
6. Right-click on the selected rows and choose “Delete Row” (or “Delete” -> “Entire Row”).  
7. Finally, clear the filter: go to the “Data” tab and click “Clear” (in the Sort & Filter group).  

The rows where the column value was zero will now be gone.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) Using a VBA Macro (for automated deletion)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
If you prefer to have a macro do it automatically, follow these steps:

1. Press Alt + F11 to open the VBA Editor.  
2. In the Project pane (usually on the left), right-click on the worksheet or workbook module where you want to place the code.  
3. Select “Insert” -> “Module.”  
4. Copy and paste the macro below into the module:  

    Sub DeleteZeroValueRows()
        Dim ws As Worksheet
        Dim lastRow As Long
        Dim i As Long
        
        ' Change "Sheet1" to the name of the worksheet you are using
        Set ws = ThisWorkbook.Sheets("Sheet1")
        
        ' Assuming the column with zeros is Column A
        ' Find the last used row in Column A
        lastRow = ws.Cells(ws.Rows.Count, "A").End(xlUp).Row
        
        ' Loop from bottom to top so row deletion won’t skip rows
        For i = lastRow To 1 Step -1
            If ws.Cells(i, "A").Value = 0 Then
                ws.Rows(i).EntireRow.Delete
            End If
        Next i
    End Sub

5. Adjust the references in the macro (for example, Sheet1 → YourSheetName, "A" → your column letter).  
6. Press Alt + F11 to return to Excel.  
7. To run the macro, go to the “Developer” tab (enable it in Options if it’s not visible) or press Alt + F8.  
8. Select the macro name (DeleteZeroValueRows) and click “Run.”  

The macro will scan the specified column and remove any row with a value of 0 in that column.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tips & Notes
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Always make a backup copy of your workbook before deleting or modifying large amounts of data.  
• If your data is in an official Excel “Table,” you can still apply the Filter approach directly.  
• Adjust the macro references (worksheet name and column letter) to match your data.  
• If you’re filtering on multiple columns, you can still apply the first method by adding multiple filter criteria before deleting rows.  

Using either of these methods, you can quickly remove rows (or entire records in a table) where a particular column equals 0.

instruction: How to achieve multiple rows of data into one row of data in Excel?
output:
Below are several approaches for transforming multiple rows of data into one row of data in Excel. Which approach you choose will depend on the structure of your source data, how you need the final result to look, and whether you wish to maintain a dynamic link (automatic updates) to the original data or just do a one-time conversion.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Using “Transpose” with Paste Special (a one-time operation)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
If you simply need to turn consecutive rows into consecutive columns—and don’t need to keep a dynamic link—try the Transpose feature:

1. Select the range of rows you want to transform into columns (a single row in your new layout).
2. Copy the selection (Ctrl + C or right-click → Copy).
3. Right-click where you want the new row to be placed.
4. Select “Paste Special…” (or in modern Excel, “Paste Special” from the drop-down).
5. Check the box labeled “Transpose” and click OK.

Note:
• This flips rows to columns (or columns to rows). If you have multiple columns, each row will become a range of cells across columns in one “block.”  
• Once pasted, the new transposed data won’t automatically update if the original data changes.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) Using TEXTJOIN or CONCAT (to combine within a single cell)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
If you want to merge each entire row into one single cell—effectively turning each row into a single string—use Excel’s TEXTJOIN or CONCAT function (Excel 2019 or later / Microsoft 365 supports TEXTJOIN):

Assume your original data is in multiple columns (A, B, C, etc.) in Row 2:
• Example row to merge: A2, B2, C2, …

Steps:
1. In a blank cell (say, D2), enter:
   =TEXTJOIN(" ", TRUE, A2:C2)  
   or  
   =CONCAT(A2," ",B2," ",C2)
   
2. This combines all cells in the range (A2:C2) separated by a space (you can pick any delimiter you like, such as comma, semicolon, or dash).

3. If you want to apply this formula to each row and then end up with a single row that lists all those merged results, you can then copy each D2, D3, D4, etc., and paste them as values in a single row.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3) Use Power Query (for structured transformations or large data)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Power Query is a robust tool (available in Excel 2016+, or as an add-in for Excel 2010/2013) that can “unpivot,” transpose, or reshape data in many ways. For example, you could:

1. Select your data → Data tab → “From Table/Range” (to bring it into Power Query).
2. Inside Power Query, use:
   • “Transpose” (Under the Transform tab) to flip rows to columns.  
   • “Combine Columns” to merge multiple columns into a single column (or “Merge Columns” function).
   • Then “Close & Load” to return data to Excel once it’s shaped exactly how you like it.

Advantages:
• You can easily refresh your transformed data if the source data changes.  
• Supports more complex transformations like adding columns, splitting, merging, filtering, grouping, etc.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4) Using a Pivot Table (depending on the original structure)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
If your data has a row-based structure that suits a pivot table (e.g., labeled headers, fields that could be aggregated), you might create a pivot table to combine values from rows. However, pivot tables generally summarize or aggregate data rather than simply transposing them, so this method is more specialized.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5) Macro/VBA Approach
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
If you frequently need to stack rows into a single row or do more fine-grained manipulations (for instance, combining rows based on certain conditions), a short VBA macro can automate the process:
1. Press Alt + F11 to open the VBA editor.
2. Insert a new Module, and paste in a VBA routine that reads each row and writes it into one row or one combined cell.
3. Run the macro when needed.

This is flexible but requires some coding knowledge.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Summary
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• If you want a simple flip from rows to columns (and vice versa) and don’t need updates, use Paste Special → Transpose.  
• If your goal is to merge multiple cells in a row into a single cell, use TEXTJOIN (or CONCAT).  
• For more advanced or dynamic transformations, consider Power Query or a pivot table if it fits your data structure.  
• If you have repeated tasks or special rules, a VBA macro can be the most efficient approach in the long run.

Choose the method that best fits your data layout, your update frequency, and how you want the final single-row data formatted.

instruction: write a detailed section about "ethical considerations during research and data analysis". List references and focus on anonymity of data, and avoiding bias
output:
Ethical Considerations During Research and Data Analysis

1. Introduction  
Ethical considerations are integral to conducting sound, credible research and ensuring the protection of participants and their data. Particularly, safeguarding anonymity and minimizing bias are critical components that help uphold the rigor, validity, and morality of the research process. This section outlines key ethical considerations relevant to ensuring participant anonymity and mitigating bias during data analysis.

2. Ensuring Anonymity of Data  
a. Informed Consent and Confidentiality. Researchers must obtain informed consent from participants, clarifying the purpose of the study and the extent to which their data will be protected (Belmont Report, 1979). This communication typically clarifies the data handling process, how anonymity is preserved, and the scope of confidentiality.  
b. Data De-Identification. Anonymity often involves the removal of all personally identifiable information (PII) from datasets. Techniques include assigning random identifiers or pseudonyms, masking direct identifiers (e.g., names, addresses), and employing aggregation methods when presenting findings (Cohen & Arieli, 2011).  
c. Secure Data Storage. Once data are de-identified, secure storage protocols—such as password-protected drives, encryption, and secure cloud-based systems—reduce the likelihood of unauthorized access or re-identification (APA, 2010).  
d. Restricted Data Access. Limiting the number of personnel with access to raw data ensures participant details remain confidential, thus respecting the privacy of subjects throughout the research lifecycle (Creswell, 2014).

3. Avoiding Bias in Data Analysis  
a. Research Design. Bias can occur at any stage of the research process, from the framing of research questions to the selection of participants. A carefully designed study with clear, well-defined methods can minimize opportunities for bias (Creswell, 2014).  
b. Blind or Double-Blind Procedures. For quantitative and qualitative research, blind or double-blind procedures reduce conscious or unconscious influences from researchers (Tokunaga, 2019). This method also diminishes the risk of selectively reporting or interpreting data in ways that favor a particular outcome.  
c. Reflexivity in Qualitative Research. In qualitative studies, reflexivity requires researchers to acknowledge their own perspectives and assumptions, helping mitigate the influence of personal biases on data interpretation (Cohen & Arieli, 2011).  
d. Data Triangulation. Combining multiple data sources or methods (e.g., quantitative surveys, qualitative interviews) can provide a more balanced perspective, reducing the effect of any single viewpoint or methodological bias (Creswell, 2014).

4. Ongoing Ethical Monitoring  
Ethical obligations extend beyond the data collection phase. Regular auditing of data handling procedures, maintaining compliance with institutional review board guidelines, and updating informed consent documents when needed are all part of ongoing ethical monitoring (APA, 2010). Researchers must remain vigilant about changing technologies and evolving ethical standards to ensure continued compliance and respect for participants.

5. Conclusion  
Ethical considerations in research and data analysis protect the integrity of the study, safeguard participants’ rights, and promote public trust in scholarly work. By emphasizing anonymity in data management and actively seeking to eliminate bias in design and analysis, researchers can address ethical implications proactively and maintain high standards of accountability.

References  
• American Psychological Association (APA). (2010). Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct. APA.  
• Belmont Report. (1979). The Belmont Report: Ethical Principles and Guidelines for the Protection of Human Subjects of Research. U.S. Department of Health, Education, and Welfare.  
• Cohen, N., & Arieli, T. (2011). Field research in conflict environments: Methodological challenges and snowball sampling. Journal of Peace Research, 48(4), 423–435.  
• Creswell, J. W. (2014). Research Design: Qualitative, Quantitative, and Mixed Methods Approaches (4th ed.). SAGE Publications.  
• Tokunaga, R. (2019). A meta-analysis of the relationships between social network site use and social support. Computers in Human Behavior, 93, 376–384.

instruction: Develop a Python program snippet to Determine High Sneezing and coughing etiquette: Preventing Spread of Germs for Engineer for Experts. Incorporate if/else or switch/case statements to handle various cases related to the Bias. Dry-run, ensure your control flow logic is clear and well-commented
output:
Below is a concise Python snippet illustrating a simple control-flow design to determine appropriate sneezing and coughing etiquette. This program uses either Python’s match/case statement (available from Python 3.10 onward) or standard if/elif/else statements to handle different “bias” cases (e.g., how intensely someone sneezes or coughs). The comments and dry-run steps clarify the logic.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Using match/case (Python >= 3.10)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
def determine_etiquette(action: str, bias: str) -> str:
    """
    Determines the best etiquette response based on a user's action
    (e.g., sneeze, cough, none) and the bias level (e.g., low, moderate, high).

    Parameters:
    -----------
    action : str
        The action performed by the user, such as 'sneeze' or 'cough'.
    bias : str
        Represents the intensity or 'bias' toward contagion or severity.
        Possible values include 'low', 'moderate', or 'high'.

    Returns:
    --------
    str
        A short instruction on the best practice to prevent germ spread.
    """
    # Normalize inputs just in case
    action = action.lower().strip()
    bias = bias.lower().strip()

    # Use match/case to handle potential actions
    match action:
        case "sneeze":
            match bias:
                case "low":
                    return "Cover your mouth/nose lightly. Wash hands or use sanitizer."
                case "moderate":
                    return ("Use elbow or tissue to cover. Dispose tissue properly. "
                            "Then wash hands thoroughly.")
                case "high":
                    return ("Wear a mask and immediately sanitize hands. "
                            "Avoid close contact with others.")
                case _:
                    return "Unrecognized bias. Practice basic sneeze etiquette."

        case "cough":
            match bias:
                case "low":
                    return "Cough into your elbow casually. Wash or sanitize hands."
                case "moderate":
                    return ("Keep your distance, cough into elbow/tissue, "
                            "and sanitize hands frequently.")
                case "high":
                    return ("Wear a mask, keep distance, cough into elbow/tissue, "
                            "discard tissue, and sanitize thoroughly.")
                case _:
                    return "Unrecognized bias. Practice basic cough etiquette."

        case "none":
            return "No sneezing or coughing. Maintain general hygiene."

        case _:
            return "Unrecognized action. Please specify 'sneeze', 'cough', or 'none'."

# Example usage:
user_action = "sneeze"         # e.g., user is sneezing
user_bias = "moderate"         # e.g., user has moderate sneezing intensity
advice = determine_etiquette(user_action, user_bias)
print(f"Advice: {advice}")


"""
Dry Run for match/case version:
--------------------------------
1) user_action = "sneeze", user_bias = "moderate"
   --> Goes to 'case "sneeze":'
   --> Within that, 'match bias:' -> 'case "moderate":'
   --> Returns: "Use elbow or tissue to cover. Dispose tissue properly. Then wash hands thoroughly."
   --> Output: "Advice: Use elbow or tissue to cover. ..."

2) If user_action = "cough", user_bias = "high"
   --> Goes to 'case "cough":'
   --> 'match bias:' -> 'case "high":'
   --> Returns: "Wear a mask, keep distance, cough into elbow/tissue, ..."

3) If user_action = "none"
   --> Goes to 'case "none":'
   --> Returns: "No sneezing or coughing. Maintain general hygiene."

4) If user_action = "random"
   --> Goes to 'case _:'
   --> Returns: "Unrecognized action..."

5) If user_bias = "extreme" (no match)
   --> Goes to 'case _:'
   --> Returns: "Unrecognized bias..."
"""


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Using if/elif/else (Compatible with all Python versions)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
def determine_etiquette_if_else(action: str, bias: str) -> str:
    """
    This version accomplishes the same task with if/elif/else blocks.
    """
    action = action.lower().strip()
    bias = bias.lower().strip()

    if action == "sneeze":
        if bias == "low":
            return "Cover your mouth/nose lightly. Wash hands or use sanitizer."
        elif bias == "moderate":
            return ("Use elbow or tissue to cover. Dispose tissue properly. "
                    "Then wash hands thoroughly.")
        elif bias == "high":
            return ("Wear a mask and immediately sanitize hands. "
                    "Avoid close contact with others.")
        else:
            return "Unrecognized bias. Practice basic sneeze etiquette."

    elif action == "cough":
        if bias == "low":
            return "Cough into your elbow casually. Wash or sanitize hands."
        elif bias == "moderate":
            return ("Keep your distance, cough into elbow/tissue, "
                    "and sanitize hands frequently.")
        elif bias == "high":
            return ("Wear a mask, keep distance, cough into elbow/tissue, "
                    "discard tissue, and sanitize thoroughly.")
        else:
            return "Unrecognized bias. Practice basic cough etiquette."

    elif action == "none":
        return "No sneezing or coughing. Maintain general hygiene."

    else:
        return "Unrecognized action. Please specify 'sneeze', 'cough', or 'none'."


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Example usage of the if/else version
    user_action = "cough"
    user_bias = "high"
    advice = determine_etiquette_if_else(user_action, user_bias)
    print(f"Advice: {advice}")

    """
    Dry Run for if/elif/else version:
    ---------------------------------
    1) user_action = "cough", user_bias = "high"
       if action == "sneeze"? No -> elif action == "cough"? Yes
       -> if bias == "low"? No
          elif bias == "moderate"? No
          elif bias == "high"? Yes
          -> returns "Wear a mask..."
       Advice printed: "Wear a mask, keep distance..."
    """

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# End of code snippet
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation:
• Both functions accept an “action” (sneeze/cough/none) and a level of “bias” (low/moderate/high).  
• match/case (Python 3.10+) allows a clean switch-like structure.  
• if/elif/else works in all versions of Python.  
• The code returns etiquette guidance depending on the combination of action and bias, helping to prevent the spread of germs.

instruction: i want to encode a video using ffmpeg and the codecs vp9 and opus. please provide me with a high quality script using the CRF function
output:
Below is a simple, high‐quality FFmpeg command that uses the VP9 video codec with CRF for quality control and Opus for audio. You can adjust the CRF value (lower = better quality, bigger output file) according to your needs. This command outputs a .webm file.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#!/usr/bin/env bash

# INPUT and OUTPUT file definitions
INPUT="input_video.mp4"
OUTPUT="output_video.webm"

# Choose a CRF value. Valid range is roughly 15–31 for VP9.
# Lower CRF = higher quality, larger file.
CRF_VALUE=20

# Audio bitrate (in kbps)
AUDIO_BITRATE=128

ffmpeg \
  -i "$INPUT" \
  -c:v libvpx-vp9 \
  -crf $CRF_VALUE \
  -b:v 0 \
  -deadline good \
  -cpu-used 0 \
  -pix_fmt yuv420p \
  -c:a libopus \
  -b:a ${AUDIO_BITRATE}k \
  "$OUTPUT"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation of the key options:

• -c:v libvpx-vp9: Selects the VP9 video codec.  
• -crf $CRF_VALUE: CRF (Constant Rate Factor) controls image quality. Lower means higher quality (and larger files).  
• -b:v 0: Tells FFmpeg to disregard average bitrate targeting and rely on CRF instead.  
• -deadline good: Balances encoding speed and quality (use best for even slower but potentially better quality).  
• -cpu-used 0: Highest quality mode (use a higher number to speed up encoding at the cost of quality).  
• -pix_fmt yuv420p: Ensures a standard pixel format, improving compatibility.  
• -c:a libopus -b:a ${AUDIO_BITRATE}k: Uses the Opus codec for audio at the specified bitrate.  

Adjust the CRF and audio bitrate to your preference. Generally, a CRF of around 15–20 provides high‐quality results. Higher than 25 begins to show noticeable artifacts, but yields smaller files.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────

CLASS 3 (10 HOURS): ADVANCED TOPICS AND EVOLUTIONARY ARCHITECTURE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Cloud-Native and Container-Based Architectures  
   • Virtual machines vs. containers vs. serverless

────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUGGESTED METHODOLOGY AND EVALUATION
