                                                    	at java.lang.Thread.run(Thread.java:1012) 
where i this erro show me how to solve this error
output:
A “java.util.concurrent.CancellationException: Task was cancelled” error typically indicates that a task executing in a thread pool or via Futures (often through methods like Future.get()) has been explicitly cancelled before it could complete. The stack trace you see:

• at X.0i9.A02(Unknown Source:32)  
• at X.0i9.get(Unknown Source:47)  
• at X.0lz.run(Unknown Source:4)  
• at X.0m4.run(Unknown Source:2)  
• at java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor.runWorker(ThreadPoolExecutor.java:1145)  
• at java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker.run(ThreadPoolExecutor.java:644)  
• at java.lang.Thread.run(Thread.java:1012)  

…shows obfuscated class names (X.0i9, X.0lz, X.0m4) and indicates the code is calling get() on a Future-like object. That call can throw CancellationException if the task was cancelled before (or during) execution.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Common Reasons This Happens
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• The Future cancel() method was deliberately called somewhere in your code (or any library code).  
• A timeout triggered a cancellation in a library or framework.  
• An external event (e.g., user action or lifecycle event in Android) might have cancelled the task.  

For example, if using Android’s AsyncTask or ExecutorService and the activity/fragment is destroyed or the user navigates away, the system may cancel background tasks. Or if a third-party library calls cancel(true) for a Future due to an error condition or lifecycle event, this will cause a CancellationException.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) How to Fix or Avoid the CancellationException
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
a) Ensure You Are Not Manually Cancelling the Task  
   • Look for calls to Future.cancel(true/false) or methods with similar names in your project or libraries.  
   • If you do need cancellation (e.g., user pressed “Stop”), then handle that case gracefully instead of letting the exception bubble up.

b) Gracefully Handle Timeouts  
   • If you use methods like future.get(timeout, timeUnit), a TimeoutException can occur. If you then cancel the task in that catch block, future.get() calls afterward may throw CancellationException.  
   • Decide whether you want to retry or skip the task.

c) Double-check Any Lifecycle-Driven Background Tasks  
   • In Android or other lifecycle-based platforms, tasks can be cancelled automatically when the activity/fragment is destroyed.  
   • Make sure you handle onDestroy(), onPause(), or other lifecycle methods and avoid calling future.get() if the context is no longer valid.

d) Wrap get() Calls with a Try/Catch to Handle Cancellations  
   • Because CancellationException (a subclass of IllegalStateException) may be thrown at runtime, add a try/catch block. For example:

     try {
         result = future.get(); // or asyncTask.get()
     } catch (CancellationException e) {
         // Handle canceled task: cleanup, logging, or ignore if that’s expected
     }

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3) Summary
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
The key idea is that you (or some library you’re using) cancelled the task (Future/AsyncTask/Runnable). The Java concurrency APIs then throw CancellationException when code subsequently tries to retrieve the result of that cancelled task. To resolve this, you need to find out:
• Why (and where) the task got cancelled.  
• Whether that cancellation is intentional or accidental.  
• If intentional, make sure you handle that flow gracefully rather than letting the CancellationException surface unhandled.  

By reviewing where cancel() might be called (in your code or library code) and by managing the task lifecycle properly, you can prevent or correctly handle this error.

instruction: for running a LLM on a local PC, what hardware will generate the most tokens per second?
output:
For most users wanting to run large language models at home (rather than in a data center), the single biggest factor in raw tokens-per-second throughput is the speed and memory capacity of the GPU. Here are the main points to consider when choosing hardware to maximize token generation speed:

1) Choose a powerful GPU with ample VRAM.  
   • High-end NVIDIA GPUs (e.g., RTX 4090, RTX 3090, or professional GPUs like A100/A6000) typically provide the best “tokens per second” on local hardware.  
   • You’ll want at least 16–24 GB of VRAM for smoother inference on many modern models (Llama-family, GPT-style models, etc.). More VRAM allows you to run larger (or higher-precision) model checkpoints.  

2) GPU architecture and memory bandwidth matter.  
   • Generating new tokens involves many matrix multiplies, which GPUs handle well. The newer the architecture (e.g., Ada Lovelace for the 40-series), the more efficient it tends to be on these workloads.  
   • The faster the GPU memory (GDDR6X vs. GDDR6), the less likely you’ll be bottlenecked by memory access.  

3) CPU is generally secondary but not irrelevant.  
   • You do need enough CPU/PCH bandwidth to feed the GPU, and a higher clock speed can help with preprocessing. Still, you’ll see the biggest performance leap when upgrading the GPU rather than the CPU.  

4) RAM is important for larger models.  
   • You’ll also want sufficient system RAM (e.g., 32–64 GB) to store the model weights (especially if you’re using off-GPU optimizations or partial loading) and to avoid swapping.  
   • If you plan to load multiple models or run them concurrently, you may need even more.  

5) Multi-GPU setups can help, but come with complications.  
   • If you can split the model across two or more GPUs, token throughput can increase. However, configuring multi-GPU inference is more complex and depends heavily on framework support, memory interconnects, and driver-level optimizations.  

In short, for most hobbyist or prosumer systems, an NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24 GB VRAM) is currently one of the fastest single-card options for local LLM inference, balancing both raw compute and VRAM capacity. If you need the absolute fastest and have no practical budget constraints (and can accommodate server-class gear at home), data-center class GPUs such as the NVIDIA A100 or H100 would offer even higher throughput. However, on a typical desktop motherboard with a single GPU, an RTX 4090 is generally the best consumer choice for maximizing “tokens per second.”

instruction: The Akkadian language only had three noun cases: Nominative, Genitive and Accusative. How were indirect objects expressed in Akkadian? Other languages use a Dative case for that but there is no Dative in Akkadian. Can you make an example that has a subject, a direct object and an indirect object? Please also show a word for word interlinear gloss for the example to show the used noun cases.
output:
In Akkadian, there is no separate Dative case; instead, indirect objects are commonly expressed with the preposition ana followed by the Genitive form of the noun. For example:

šarrum iddin kaspam ana awīlim  
---------------------------------------------------
šarrum  | king(NOM)     | “the king”  
iddin   | give(3ms.PRET)| “(he) gave”  
kaspam  | silver(ACC)   | “silver”  
ana     | to            | “to”  
awīlim  | man(GEN)      | “the man”  

In this sentence, šarrum “king(NOM)” is the subject, kaspam “silver(ACC)” is the direct object, and the indirect object “to the man” is expressed via the preposition ana plus awīlim in the Genitive case.

instruction: Translate into rigorous Lojban: I am talking about Paris in English to someone related to Jane who about to write a letter.
output:
Here is one clear way to render it in Lojban, using two chained relative clauses on “the person”:

mi tavla lo prenu poi srana la dji,n. ku poi pu’o ciska lo xatra la paris. la gliban.

Explanation of structure:

• mi tavla = “I talk/speak”  
• lo prenu poi srana la dji,n. ku = “to a person who is related to Jane”  
• poi pu’o ciska lo xatra = “who is about to write (pu’o) a letter (xatra)”  
• la paris. = “about Paris”  
• la gliban. = “in the English language.”  

The place structure for tavla (x1 tavla x2 x3 x4) is:  
1) the speaker,  
2) the audience,  
3) the topic,  
4) the language.  

Hence, “mi tavla lo prenu … la paris. la gliban.” means “I speak to that person about Paris in English,” with the two relative clauses (poi srana la dji,n. and poi pu’o ciska lo xatra) further describing that person.

instruction: Craft me a deep learning curriculum
output:
Below is a structured, step-by-step deep learning curriculum that covers foundational concepts, core techniques, and advanced applications. The curriculum is designed to accommodate different learning paces and backgrounds. It starts with mathematical and machine learning fundamentals, then moves toward specialized deep learning topics, implementation skills, and research. Each module includes suggested reading, hands-on assignments, and practice ideas.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. FOUNDATIONS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1.1 Mathematics and Statistics Refresher
• Linear Algebra: vectors, matrices, matrix multiplication, eigenvalues/eigenvectors, singular value decomposition (SVD).  
• Calculus: differentiation, partial derivatives, chain rule, gradient.  
• Probability and Statistics: random variables, expectations, distributions, maximum likelihood estimation, basics of hypothesis testing.  

Suggested Resources
• Linear Algebra – YouTube channels like 3Blue1Brown or Khan Academy.  
• Mathematics for Machine Learning (Deisenroth et al.).  
• A refresher in Probability and Statistics – Khan Academy or StatQuest on YouTube.  

Practice
• Solve basic linear algebra and calculus exercises by hand.  
• Use NumPy to practice vector and matrix operations.  

1.2 Machine Learning Fundamentals
• Supervised vs. unsupervised learning paradigms.  
• Performance metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, confusion matrix, Mean Squared Error (MSE), etc.  
• Bias–variance tradeoff, regularization (L1, L2, dropout concept).  
• Gradient-based optimization (Stochastic Gradient Descent, momentum, Adam).  

Suggested Resources
• “Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras, and TensorFlow” by Aurélien Géron (first few chapters).  
• Andrew Ng’s Coursera course: “Machine Learning.”  

Practice
• Implement simple ML models (linear regression, logistic regression) in Python.  
• Familiarize yourself with scikit-learn for classical ML models.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. INTRODUCTION TO NEURAL NETWORKS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

2.1 Neural Network Basics
• Biological inspiration and history (Perceptron, MLPs, backpropagation).  
• Components of a feedforward network: input, hidden, output layers.  
• Activation functions (ReLU, Sigmoid, Tanh, Leaky ReLU, etc.).  
• Loss functions (cross-entropy, MSE).  

Suggested Resources
• “Deep Learning” by Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio, and Aaron Courville (Chapters on MLPs and backpropagation).  

Practice
• Implement a simple feedforward neural network (e.g., MNIST digit classification) from scratch using NumPy.  
• Experiment with different activation functions and see how they affect training.  

2.2 Framework Familiarization
• Introduction to modern deep learning frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX).  
• Tensors, computational graphs, automatic differentiation.  
• Basic data loading and preprocessing best practices.  

Suggested Resources
• Official tutorials of the chosen framework (e.g., PyTorch official tutorials).  
• “Deep Learning with PyTorch” by Eli Stevens, Luca Antiga, and Thomas Viehmann, if you choose PyTorch.  

Practice
• Replicate a basic feedforward network from scratch, but now using a deep learning framework.  
• Explore a standard dataset (e.g., MNIST or CIFAR-10) using data loaders.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. CONVOLUTIONAL NEURAL NETWORKS (CNNs)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

3.1 CNN Architecture and Concepts
• Convolution operations: kernels, strides, padding.  
• Pooling (max pooling, average pooling), fully connected layers, flattening.  
• Popular CNN architectures: LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, ResNet, DenseNet.  

Suggested Resources
• Papers describing classical architectures (e.g., “ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks” by Krizhevsky et al.).  
• “Hands-On Computer Vision with TensorFlow 2” by Benjamin Planche and Eliot Andres, or relevant sections in deep learning textbooks.  

Practice
• Implement a CNN for image classification on CIFAR-10.  
• Experiment with deeper networks, try data augmentation to improve results.  

3.2 Practical Tricks and Techniques for CNNs
• Batch normalization, dropout, residual connections.  
• Transfer learning and fine-tuning.  
• Modern data augmentation strategies (random crop, random flip, color jitter, mixup, Cutout, etc.).  

Suggested Resources
• “Bag of Tricks for Image Classification with Convolutional Neural Networks” by T. He et al.  
• Various online guides for PyTorch/TensorFlow regarding data augmentation.  

Practice
• Fine-tune a pre-trained model (ResNet, VGG) on a smaller dataset (e.g., flowers dataset).  
• Compare training from scratch vs. transfer learning.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. SEQUENCE MODELS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

4.1 Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs)
• The need for sequence modeling.  
• RNN architecture and backpropagation through time.  
• Vanishing and exploding gradients problem.  

Suggested Resources
• Section on RNNs in “Deep Learning” (Goodfellow et al.).  
• Blog posts by Colah (Christopher Olah) on RNNs and LSTMs.  

Practice
• Implement an RNN from scratch for a simple time-series prediction (e.g., sinusoidal data).  
• Visualize gradient flows and see how vanishing gradients occur.  

4.2 LSTM and GRU
• LSTM components (input gate, forget gate, output gate).  
• GRU architecture and differences from LSTM.  
• Use cases: text classification, language modeling, speech recognition.  

Suggested Resources
• “Understanding LSTM Networks” by Colah’s blog.  
• Tutorials on LSTM/GRU in PyTorch or TensorFlow.  

Practice
• Build a language model that predicts the next word in a sentence.  
• Train a sentiment analysis model on text data using LSTM or GRU.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. ATTENTION MECHANISMS & TRANSFORMERS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

5.1 Transformers and Self-Attention
• Attention mechanism overview and motivation.  
• Scaled dot-product attention, multi-head self-attention.  
• Positional encoding, feedforward sub-layers, and layer normalization.  

Suggested Resources
• “Attention Is All You Need” (Vaswani et al.).  
• “The Illustrated Transformer” blog post by Jay Alammar.  

Practice
• Implement a simple machine translation model using a Transformer architecture.  
• Use a library (e.g., Hugging Face Transformers) to train or fine-tune a BERT or GPT model on a downstream NLP task.  

5.2 Large Language Models (LLMs)
• BERT, GPT family, T5, and others.  
• Tokenization strategies (WordPiece, Byte-Pair Encoding) and masked language modeling.  
• Prompt engineering and fine-tuning best practices.  

Suggested Resources
• Hugging Face Transformers documentation.  
• Research papers such as “BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding” and GPT papers by OpenAI.  

Practice
• Fine-tune a pre-trained LLM for sentiment classification or question answering.  
• Experiment with prompt engineering for zero-shot or few-shot tasks.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. MODEL OPTIMIZATIONS AND TRAINING BEST PRACTICES
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

6.1 Effective Training Techniques
• Weight initialization methods (Xavier, He).  
• Learning rate scheduling (exponential decay, cyclical learning rates, warm restarts).  
• Regularization: dropout, weight decay, label smoothing.  
• Hyperparameter tuning (grid search, random search, Bayesian optimization).  

Suggested Resources
• Deep Learning framework documentation on scheduling and optimization.  
• Blogs/papers on hyperparameter search techniques (e.g., Google Vizier).  

Practice
• Experiment with different learning rate schedules on a CNN or RNN model.  
• Tune hyperparameters for best performance on a validation set.  

6.2 Model Deployment
• Model compression (quantization, pruning, knowledge distillation).  
• Serving frameworks (TensorFlow Serving, TorchServe, ONNX Runtime).  
• Scaling and containerization with Docker, Kubernetes.  

Suggested Resources
• Official TensorFlow Serving / TorchServe docs.  
• Papers like “Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network” (Hinton et al.) for knowledge distillation.  

Practice
• Convert a PyTorch model to ONNX, test inference speed in different environments.  
• Deploy a simple web API using Flask/FastAPI to serve a trained model.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. UNCERTAINTY, INTERPRETABILITY, AND ETHICS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

7.1 Interpretability
• Feature importance methods (Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME).  
• Interpretable modeling for critical domains (medical, finance).  

Suggested Resources
• Papers on SHAP, LIME, and Grad-CAM.  
• “Interpretable Machine Learning” by Christoph Molnar.  

Practice
• Use Grad-CAM on a CNN to visualize where the model is “looking” for classifications.  
• Apply SHAP or LIME to get explanations for an NLP model’s predictions.  

7.2 Ethical Considerations
• Data bias and fairness in AI.  
• Privacy, data protection (GDPR, etc.).  
• Societal impact, job displacement, accountability, transparency.  

Suggested Resources
• “Weapons of Math Destruction” by Cathy O’Neil.  
• “The Ethical Algorithm” by Michael Kearns and Aaron Roth.  

Practice
• Perform a bias check on a classification model with unbalanced data.  
• Implement data anonymization techniques where required.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
8. ADVANCED TOPICS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

8.1 Generative Models
• Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs).  
• Applications: image synthesis, style transfer, data augmentation.  

Suggested Resources
• Original GAN paper: “Generative Adversarial Nets” (Goodfellow et al.).  
• Tutorials on VAEs and GANs in PyTorch/TensorFlow.  

Practice
• Implement a simple VAE to generate MNIST digits.  
• Train a basic DCGAN to synthesize images.  

8.2 Reinforcement Learning (RL) with Deep Learning
• Value-based methods (DQN).  
• Policy-based methods (REINFORCE, PPO).  
• Environments: OpenAI Gym.  

Suggested Resources
• “Deep Reinforcement Learning Hands-On” by Maxim Lapan.  
• “Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction” by Sutton & Barto (focus on deep RL sections).  

Practice
• Implement a DQN to solve a simple game like CartPole in OpenAI Gym.  
• Experiment with advanced algorithms like PPO or A2C.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
9. TAKE IT TO RESEARCH AND PRACTICE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

9.1 Reading Research Papers
• Best practice for reading research – understand abstract, introduction, methodology, results, discussion.  
• Following top conferences: NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, CVPR, ECCV, ICCV, ACL, EMNLP.  
• ArXiv preprints for the latest developments.  

Practice
• Summarize new papers, replicate experiments on open-sourced code.  
• Contribute to open-source deep learning repositories.  

9.2 Building a Portfolio & Open-Source Contributions
• Showcasing projects on GitHub/GitLab; writing readme docs.  
• Kaggle competitions for practical experience.  
• Contributing bug fixes or new features to open-source initiatives (e.g., PyTorch, TensorFlow, Hugging Face).  

Practice
• Maintain a GitHub portfolio of personal and collaborative projects.  
• Engage in Kaggle competitions, measure progress.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ADDITIONAL TIPS FOR SUCCESS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Stay organized with a learning plan or schedule.  
• Engage in online communities or study groups (Reddit r/MachineLearning, Kaggle forums, etc.).  
• Practice coding daily; small consistent practice is more effective than sporadic large efforts.  
• Keep experimenting with different hyperparameters, architectures, and frameworks to deepen intuition.  
• Publish your results, failures, and insights in blog posts; teaching is an excellent way to solidify understanding.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CONCLUSION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
This curriculum offers a roadmap to mastering deep learning, beginning with solid mathematical and machine learning foundations and progressing through core neural network concepts, advanced architectures, and real-world deployment strategies. By combining theoretical understanding with hands-on implementation and experimentation, you’ll develop the intuition and problem-solving skills essential for success in deep learning projects and research.  

Good luck, and enjoy your deep learning journey!

instruction: Can you show me a transfer learning example with python code.
output:
Below is a minimal end-to-end example of transfer learning in Python using TensorFlow/Keras. This walkthrough uses the VGG16 model pretrained on ImageNet as a “base model,” then adds a new classifier on top to fine-tune for a small sample dataset (here we use CIFAR-10 for demonstration).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Transfer Learning Example with TensorFlow/Keras
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras.applications import VGG16
from tensorflow.keras import layers, models
from tensorflow.keras.datasets import cifar10
from tensorflow.keras.utils import to_categorical

# 1. Load and prepare data
#    CIFAR-10 has 50k training and 10k test images of shape (32, 32, 3).
(x_train, y_train), (x_test, y_test) = cifar10.load_data()

# Convert pixel values [0,255] to [0,1] by dividing by 255.0
x_train = x_train.astype('float32') / 255.0
x_test  = x_test.astype('float32') / 255.0

# Convert labels to one-hot encoding
y_train = to_categorical(y_train, 10)
y_test  = to_categorical(y_test, 10)

# 2. Define the base model (VGG16)
#    By default, VGG16 expects 224x224 images. 
#    We can resize from (32,32) to (224,224) on-the-fly in a pipeline,
#    or explicitly, for simplicity shown below (this can be memory intensive).
resize_layer = tf.keras.layers.Lambda(
    lambda image: tf.image.resize(image, (224, 224))
)

# We exclude VGG16's final classification layers by setting include_top=False.
# We also set input_shape to (224, 224, 3), which matches our resized images.
base_model = VGG16(weights='imagenet', include_top=False, input_shape=(224, 224, 3))

# Freeze all layers in base_model so their weights do not get updated during training.
for layer in base_model.layers:
    layer.trainable = False

# 3. Build a new model on top of the base_model
model = models.Sequential()
# Resize CIFAR-10 images from (32,32) to (224,224)
model.add(resize_layer)
# Add the pretrained VGG16 base
model.add(base_model)
# Flatten the output of the convolutional base
model.add(layers.Flatten())
# Add custom classifier layers
model.add(layers.Dense(256, activation='relu'))
model.add(layers.Dropout(0.5))
model.add(layers.Dense(10, activation='softmax'))

# 4. Compile the model
model.compile(
    loss='categorical_crossentropy',
    optimizer=tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=1e-4),
    metrics=['accuracy']
)

# 5. Train the model
#    Note: If you have limited compute, you might reduce epochs or batch size.
model.fit(
    x_train, y_train,
    validation_data=(x_test, y_test),
    epochs=3,
    batch_size=64
)

# 6. Evaluate the model
test_loss, test_acc = model.evaluate(x_test, y_test, verbose=0)
print(f"Test accuracy: {test_acc:.3f}, Test loss: {test_loss:.3f}")

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Explanation of Key Steps
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Loading and preprocessing data:
   • We use the CIFAR-10 dataset. The images are 32×32 pixels, which is smaller than the 224×224 expected by VGG16. Therefore, we use a resizing layer to match the input shape required by VGG16 (224×224).

2) Building the base model:
   • VGG16 (pretrained on ImageNet) is used as the “base” network. Setting include_top=False removes the fully connected layers (the classifier) from VGG16, leaving only the convolutional base for feature extraction.

3) Freezing the base model’s layers:
   • We freeze (set trainable = False) the existing layers so that the pretrained weights do not change during training. This keeps the general feature extraction intact.

4) Adding custom classification layers:
   • After flattening the features from the base model, we add new Dense layers to tailor the model to our 10-class CIFAR-10 task.

5) Compiling and training:
   • We use Adam optimizer with a low learning rate and train for a few epochs.

6) Evaluation:
   • We finally check the test set accuracy and loss. With fine-tuning (unfreezing a few of the deeper layers in the base model) or more epochs, you can improve performance further.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Tips for Real-World Applications
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
• Fine-Tuning: Instead of freezing all base layers, try “fine-tuning.” You can unfreeze some top layers of the base model to adapt them more precisely to your new task—but keep an eye on overfitting and choose a very low learning rate.  
• Data Augmentation: When your dataset is small, image augmentations (random flips, rotations, color jitter) help improve generalization.  
• Preprocessing: Always ensure you match the model’s standardized preprocessing (e.g., means and scaling) when you feed images into the pretrained network. TensorFlow/Keras provides built-in utilities in tf.keras.applications.imagenet_utils or tf.keras.applications.vgg16.preprocess_input.  
• Hardware: Transfer learning can be computationally intensive. Use a GPU (or TPU) if available for faster training.

This code gives a high-level idea of how to apply transfer learning using a pretrained model. Adjust hyperparameters (batch size, number of epochs, learning rate) and consider dataset-specific transformations or augmentations for best results.

instruction: show me example of how to cross validate by using shuffle split in sklearn
output:
Below is a simple example of using ShuffleSplit for cross-validation in scikit-learn. This example uses the Iris dataset and a LogisticRegression model, but you can adapt it to your own data and model.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Example: Using ShuffleSplit with LogisticRegression on the Iris dataset
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import ShuffleSplit, cross_val_score

# 1. Load sample data (Iris dataset)
X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)

# 2. Define the ShuffleSplit cross-validator
#    - n_splits = number of re-shuffling & splitting iterations
#    - test_size = proportion of the dataset to include in the test split
#    - random_state = fixed seed for reproducibility
cv = ShuffleSplit(n_splits=5, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)

# 3. Define a model to be evaluated
model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=200)

# 4. Perform cross-validation using ShuffleSplit
scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=cv)

# 5. Print each split score and the average
print("Cross-validation scores (each split):", scores)
print("Mean cross-validation score:", scores.mean())

Explanation:
• ShuffleSplit randomly splits the dataset into training and test sets multiple times (n_splits). 
• Each split uses a test_size proportion of the data for testing and the remainder for training.
• cross_val_score takes a model, your features (X), labels (y), and the cross-validator instance (cv) to run and evaluate the model multiple times. 
• The returned array (scores) holds the scores for each split. They can then be averaged to get an overall performance metric.

instruction: I am building XGBoost classifier and i want to see partial dependence plots using shap for top important variables. give me code.
output:
Below is a minimal end-to-end example showing how to train an XGBoost classifier, compute SHAP values, identify the most important features using SHAP summary plots, and then create SHAP-based “partial dependence” (more precisely, SHAP dependence) plots for the top features. You can adapt this code to your own dataset.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Install required libraries (if needed)

pip install xgboost shap

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2) Example code

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xgboost as xgb
import shap
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# --------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data (example uses breast cancer dataset)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------
data = load_breast_cancer()
X = pd.DataFrame(data.data, columns=data.feature_names)
y = data.target

# Split into train/test for demonstration
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42
)

# --------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Train an XGBoost classifier
# --------------------------------------------------------------------
model = xgb.XGBClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=42)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# --------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Create a SHAP explainer and compute SHAP values
# --------------------------------------------------------------------
# For tree-based models (like XGBoost), we use TreeExplainer
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(model)
# Depending on SHAP version, you might use shap_values = explainer.shap_values(X_train) or .values
# The general approach in newer versions is .shap_values(), but some older code uses .values
shap_values = explainer.shap_values(X_train)

# --------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Identify top important features using SHAP summary plot
#    (this plot shows global importance of features)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------
shap.summary_plot(shap_values, X_train)

# From the summary plot, pick the top N features you want to investigate further. 
# Suppose you see "mean radius", "mean texture", "mean perimeter" as top features.

# --------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Plot SHAP dependence ("partial dependence") for top features
# --------------------------------------------------------------------
# shap.dependence_plot(feature, shap_values, X, interaction_index=None)
# will show how that feature’s value impacts its SHAP value across the dataset.
# You can also set interaction_index to another feature to see 2D interactions.

top_features = ["mean radius", "mean texture", "mean perimeter"]  # Replace with your top features

for feat in top_features:
    shap.dependence_plot(feat, shap_values, X_train)

# Alternatively, for truly “partial dependence” style plots (which integrate out
# other features) SHAP includes shap.plots.partial_dependence for some versions:

# shap.plots.partial_dependence(
#     feature="mean radius",
#     model.predict,
#     X_train,
#     ice=False,  # True would display ICE curves
#     model_expected_value=True
# )

# The above partial_dependence API may vary by SHAP version. Check SHAP’s docs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Notes on SHAP Plots

• shap.summary_plot(shap_values, X_train) displays the overall feature importance, as well as how features drive predictions in a global manner.  
• shap.dependence_plot(feature, shap_values, X_train) is typically referred to as a “SHAP dependence plot.” It shows how variations in one specific feature affect its SHAP values (i.e., the feature’s contribution to the prediction), with color encoding another feature by default.  
• shap.plots.partial_dependence (available in newer versions of SHAP) can generate a classical partial dependence plot, integrating out other features. This function takes a model-prediction function (e.g., model.predict), the dataset, and the feature name(s).  

Adjust the above code to suit your dataset and the SHAP version you have installed.

instruction: You are a DM running 5th Edition D&D. Before you begin your campaign, you want to bring some of the most powerful spells down to a more reasonable power level. Which spells do you change and how?
output:
Below are a few commonly cited “problem” or overly powerful spells in Fifth Edition D&D, along with suggested tweaks for bringing them back in line. Of course, the exact adjustments depend on your table’s tastes, so think of these as a starting point rather than hard-and-fast rules.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Wish
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• The Issue: Wish is famously open-ended and can overshadow entire adventures with a single casting. Even the “safe” uses (replicating 8th-level or lower spells) are extremely powerful and flexible.  
• Possible Tweaks:
  – Limit it to the “replicate a lower-level spell” effect only. If a player wants to attempt a custom effect, treat it like a magical ritual that requires downtime, a special location, or material components worth a considerable sum—and impose story-driven repercussions.  
  – Reinforce the stress penalty. Rules as written, a 33% chance exists (d100 roll of 33 or less) that you lose the ability to cast Wish again. If you want to make Wish less common, lower that threshold to something like 50%, or add immediate detrimental effects (exhaustion, HP maximum reduction, etc.) every time the spell is cast.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Simulacrum
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• The Issue: Simulacrum effectively doubles a high-level spellcaster’s power with few drawbacks (the clone can cast the original’s spell slots).  
• Possible Tweaks:
  – Limit Simulacrum’s target to creatures of CR 10 or lower, or “humanoid creatures up to level 10.” This caps the potency.  
  – Enforce the “it can’t regain spell slots” rule more tightly by clarifying that no item or effect (like a short rest or consumable magic item) can circumvent the inability to regain spell slots.  
  – Reduce Simulacrum’s HP to half (or even a quarter) of the original creature. This makes the copy far more fragile.  
  – Impose high maintenance costs or frequent “stabilizing” rituals; e.g., the simulacrum must be re-infused with rare materials every week or month or it disappears.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. True Polymorph
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• The Issue: True Polymorph allows effectively permanent transformation, enabling certain game-breaking combos—like turning peasants into dragons or items into powerful creatures.  
• Possible Tweaks:
  – Restrict the allowable CR for a transformation; for example, “You can only transform a creature into another creature of CR equal to or less than half its original CR or level.”  
  – Remove the permanent duration. Make the spell last until dispelled, requiring concentration or a special ritual to maintain beyond its initial casting time.  
  – Emphasize that any mental ability scores or class features only transform if the DM allows. If you keep it purely a “physical” transformation, you avoid messy intelligence or spellcasting gains.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Conjure X Spells (Conjure Animals, Conjure Woodland Beings, Conjure Minor Elementals, etc.)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• The Issue: These spells provide action economy advantages: a single caster can flood the battlefield with multiple creatures, slowing combat and overshadowing other party members.  
• Possible Tweaks:
  – Limit the maximum number of creatures to a smaller amount. For example, Conjure Animals might only summon up to two beasts of CR 1 or lower, instead of eight.  
  – Remove the randomness. Instead of “the DM chooses,” rewrite it so the spell text states exactly what creatures you can summon for each spell level (and keep that list short).  
  – Maintain concentration requirements more strictly; if the caster is damaged, has to make multiple concentration checks, or tries to maintain multiple concentration spells via magic items, be vigilant that they are following the normal 5e rules.  
  – Have the summoned creatures (especially fey) demand something in return, or not obey automatically each round unless the caster uses a bonus action to command them.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. Banishment
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• The Issue: A single save-or-suck that can remove an enemy from the fight entirely (especially creatures from other planes).  
• Possible Tweaks:
  – Allow a repeated saving throw at the end of each of the banished creature’s turns. This makes it similar in feel to other strong control spells (like Hold Person or Hold Monster).  
  – Restrict its duration. Instead of Concentration, up to 1 minute, consider reducing it to Concentration, up to a number of rounds equal to your spellcasting ability modifier.  
  – Require a more specific target type, e.g., “a creature native to a plane other than your own.”  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Forcecage
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• The Issue: Forcecage can trap many creatures instantly with no saving throw and no concentration.  
• Possible Tweaks:
  – Require a Dexterity saving throw to avoid being enclosed when the cage appears.  
  – Require concentration to keep Forcecage active; if you lose focus, the cage collapses.  
  – Increase the material component cost or make it a consumable focus (e.g., the components are consumed during casting).  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Silvery Barbs (optional, from Strixhaven)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• The Issue: Silvery Barbs is very inexpensive for a 1st-level spell, simultaneously imposing disadvantage and handing out advantage, especially when combined with reaction-based combos.  
• Possible Tweaks:
  – Raise its level from 1st to 2nd, or require a spell slot equal to or higher than the spell you are interrupting.  
  – Limit its advantage effect to the caster themselves (no handing out advantage to an ally).  
  – Impose a small resource cost, such as requiring a spellcasting focus that is consumed or giving the caster one level of exhaustion if used repeatedly in a single day.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
8. Other Considerations
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Polymorph: Many GMs already treat Polymorph carefully. You could cap the maximum CR, especially for non-self-targets, or reduce the hit points gained upon transformation.  
• Healing Spirit (Xanathar’s Guide to Everything): If you use older printings, it was often spammed between combats for large team-wide healing. You might limit the number of uses per cast or require a bonus action to heal a single target on the caster’s turn only.  
• Guidance: Although not a huge balance-breaker, some tables feel it becomes the constant “tap for +1d4” to every ability check. You can rule that it can’t be cast if the caster or the target is in initiative, or enforce that the target must be willing and actively focusing on the spell (meaning it can’t be done reflexively all the time).  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
In Summary
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
When homebrewing or house-ruling spells, transparency with your players is key. Let them know what you’re changing (and why) before the campaign starts. If you impose limitations that feel fair and consistent, you’ll preserve the spirit of these iconic spells without letting them become so dominant that they overshadow everyone else’s play. And, if something doesn’t work, remain open to adjusting mid-campaign in a fair way that preserves everyone’s fun.

instruction: Convert the Pathfinder Cryptic class to 5e D&D.  Incorporate as many of the class features for all levels while following the normal level progression, i.e. every 4 levels there is an Ability Score Improvement. within the first 3 levels, the player should be able to choose the subclass archetype.
output:
Below is a homebrew conversion of the Pathfinder “Cryptic” class into Dungeons & Dragons 5th Edition rules. This is not official 5e content, but rather a suggested framework to capture the Cryptic’s flavor—manipulating hidden patterns and exploiting weaknesses—within 5e’s familiar class structure. GMs and players should freely adjust any part of this to best fit their table’s balance and thematic needs.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CLASS OVERVIEW
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The Cryptic is a studious, perceptive adept who sees the hidden “code” of reality. By discerning and manipulating these underlying patterns, they can expose vulnerabilities in foes, craft illusions, and alter the flow of magic and psionic energies around them. Cryptics often specialize in a particular approach to pattern manipulation, reflected in their Archetype choice at 3rd level.

QUICK BUILD
• Choose Intelligence as your highest ability score, followed by Dexterity or Wisdom.  
• Pick a background that emphasizes study or investigation (e.g., Sage or Inquisitive).  
• Select cantrips and spells (if using optional Psionic/Arcane progression) or focus on skill usage that reflects your insight into hidden phenomena.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CLASS FEATURES
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Hit Points  
• Hit Die: 1d8 per Cryptic level  
• Hit Points at 1st Level: 8 + your Constitution modifier  
• Hit Points at Higher Levels: 1d8 (or 5) + your Constitution modifier per Cryptic level after 1st  

Proficiencies  
• Armor: Light armor  
• Weapons: Simple weapons, one or two specific martial weapons (your choice) that reflect your cryptic training (e.g., rapier or scimitar)  
• Tools: Choose one from Thieves’ tools or a relevant artisan's tool (e.g., calligrapher’s supplies if your Cryptic focuses on runes/patterns)  
• Saving Throws: Intelligence, Dexterity  
• Skills: Choose two from Arcana, Deception, Investigation, Perception, Persuasion, Sleight of Hand, Stealth  

Equipment  
You start with the following equipment, in addition to the equipment granted by your background:  
• (a) a rapier or (b) a quarterstaff or (c) a dagger and a light crossbow with 20 bolts  
• (a) a scholar’s pack or (b) an explorer’s pack  
• Leather armor, a simple melee weapon, and a set of tools you are proficient with  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
THE CRYPTIC
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The Cryptic progression table is summarized below. Reference the descriptions of each feature afterward.

Level | Proficiency Bonus | Class Features
1     | +2 | Disrupt Pattern, Cryptic Cipher
2     | +2 | Esoteric Insight (1 option), Read Patterns
3     | +2 | Cryptic Archetype, Cryptic Archetype Feature
4     | +2 | Ability Score Improvement
5     | +3 | Disrupt Pattern (Extra Die), Esoteric Insight (2 options)
6     | +3 | Unraveling Stare
7     | +3 | Cryptic Archetype Feature
8     | +3 | Ability Score Improvement
9     | +4 | Disrupt Pattern (Extra Die), Esoteric Insight (3 options)
10    | +4 | Veiled Mind
11    | +4 | Cryptic Archetype Feature
12    | +4 | Ability Score Improvement
13    | +5 | Disrupt Pattern (Extra Die), Esoteric Insight (4 options)
14    | +5 | Pattern Warp
15    | +5 | Cryptic Archetype Feature
16    | +5 | Ability Score Improvement
17    | +6 | Disrupt Pattern (Extra Die), Esoteric Insight (5 options)
18    | +6 | Bypass Reality
19    | +6 | Ability Score Improvement
20    | +6 | Apex of Patterns, Cryptic Archetype Capstone

Below are the class features in detail.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1ST LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Disrupt Pattern
Starting at 1st level, you learn to perceive and exploit the hidden flaws in a creature’s “pattern.” When you hit a creature with a weapon attack or a Cryptic feature (such as a cantrip or class-based ability, if your DM allows you to use psionic or magical attacks for this feature), you deal an additional 1d4 psychic damage.  
• This extra damage increases as you gain levels in this class, reflected in the “Disrupt Pattern (Extra Die)” rows in the Cryptic table: at 5th level and every 4 levels thereafter (9th, 13th, 17th), the die increases by one step on this scale: 1d4 → 1d6 → 1d8 → 1d10 → 1d12.  
• You can deal this extra damage once per turn.

Cryptic Cipher
Also at 1st level, you have studied unique ciphers, illusions, or mental constructs that grant you specialized knowledge. Choose one of the following benefits (or another thematic feature that your DM approves):  
• Cipher of Deception: You gain proficiency in Deception (if you already have it, choose another skill from the Cryptic skill list). Additionally, you have advantage on checks made to pass hidden messages via illusions, code, or misdirection.  
• Cipher of Insight: You gain proficiency in Investigation (or another skill of your choice if already proficient). When you Investigate magical or psionic phenomena, you may add double your proficiency bonus to the ability check.  
• Cipher of Stealth: You gain proficiency in Stealth (or choose from the Cryptic skill list if already proficient). Additionally, you can attempt to Hide even when you are only lightly obscured, representing your ability to blend into the patterns of your surroundings.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2ND LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Esoteric Insight (1 option at 2nd level)
You learn one specialized trick that further enhances your pattern manipulation. Choose one of the following Esoteric Insights, or work with your DM to craft a similar option. You gain additional Esoteric Insights at higher levels (2 at 5th, 3 at 9th, 4 at 13th, 5 at 17th). Once chosen, they cannot be changed.

Examples of Esoteric Insights:
• Pattern Blindside: As a bonus action, you can force a target within 60 feet to make a Wisdom saving throw (DC = 8 + your proficiency bonus + your Intelligence modifier). On a failure, the target can’t see you until the start of your next turn (though it is aware of your location unless hidden).  
• Warp Sensory Input: As an action, choose one creature within 30 feet. That creature has disadvantage on the next Perception or Investigation check it makes within 1 minute.  
• Mental Echo: When you deal psychic damage with Disrupt Pattern, you can create a mental echo that lasts until your next turn. If the target makes an attack against you before then, it takes 1d4 psychic damage (no action required from you).  
• Rune Trap: As an action, you create a small glyph on a surface. The first creature (other than you) that enters or starts its turn within 5 feet of the glyph must succeed on a Dexterity saving throw (DC as above) or take 1d8 force damage. The glyph vanishes after it triggers or after 1 minute.

Read Patterns
You can spend 1 minute observing a creature, object, or area to discern subtle energies or hidden markings. At the end of that minute, you can ask the DM one question about the subject’s nature, vulnerabilities, resistances, recent magical influences, or similar pattern-based information. The DM will provide a truthful but possibly cryptic answer.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3RD LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Cryptic Archetype
Choose an archetype that reflects your specialized approach to pattern manipulation. Three sample archetypes are detailed later: Pattern Breaker, Psyche Shaper, and Reality Hacker. Your choice grants you features at 3rd level, and again at 7th, 11th, 15th, and 20th levels.

Cryptic Archetype Feature  
When you choose your archetype at 3rd level, you immediately gain a unique ability granted by that archetype. (See “Sample Cryptic Archetypes” below.)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4TH LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Ability Score Improvement
When you reach 4th level, and again at 8th, 12th, 16th, and 19th levels, you can increase one ability score of your choice by 2, or you can increase two ability scores of your choice by 1. As normal, you can’t increase an ability score above 20 using this feature.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5TH LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Disrupt Pattern (Extra Die)  
Your Disrupt Pattern damage die increases from 1d4 to 1d6.

Esoteric Insight (2 options)  
You gain your second Esoteric Insight.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6TH LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Unraveling Stare
You gain the ability to momentarily strip away defenses. As a bonus action, choose one creature you can see within 60 feet. That creature’s AC is reduced by 2 (to a minimum of 10) until the end of your next turn.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7TH LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Cryptic Archetype Feature  
You gain a feature from your chosen archetype.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
8TH LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Ability Score Improvement  
You gain the standard ASI for 8th level.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
9TH LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Disrupt Pattern (Extra Die)  
Your Disrupt Pattern damage die increases from 1d6 to 1d8.

Esoteric Insight (3 options)  
You gain a third Esoteric Insight.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
10TH LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Veiled Mind
Your mind is shielded by layered patterns. You have advantage on saving throws against effects that sense, read, or control thoughts (such as detect thoughts or dominate person). Additionally, creatures trying to read your emotions or surface thoughts have disadvantage on their ability checks to do so.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
11TH LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Cryptic Archetype Feature
You gain another feature from your archetype.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
12TH LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Ability Score Improvement (ASI)  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
13TH LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Disrupt Pattern (Extra Die)  
Your Disrupt Pattern damage die increases from 1d8 to 1d10.

Esoteric Insight (4 options)  
You gain a fourth Esoteric Insight.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
14TH LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Pattern Warp
As a bonus action, you twist local reality for 1 minute. For the duration, you gain one of the following benefits (choose upon using this feature):  
• You gain a +2 bonus to AC.  
• You gain advantage on Dexterity saving throws.  
• You can move through other creatures’ spaces without provoking opportunity attacks.  
Once you use this feature, you can’t use it again until you finish a short or long rest.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
15TH LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Cryptic Archetype Feature
You gain another feature from your archetype.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
16TH LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Ability Score Improvement (ASI)  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
17TH LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Disrupt Pattern (Extra Die)  
Your Disrupt Pattern damage die increases from 1d10 to 1d12.

Esoteric Insight (5 options)  
You gain your fifth Esoteric Insight.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
18TH LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Bypass Reality
You can briefly slip between the cracks of reality. As a bonus action, you become intangible and invisible until the start of your next turn. During this time, you can move through creatures and objects as if they were difficult terrain; if you end your turn inside an object, you are immediately shunted to the nearest unoccupied space and take 1d10 force damage. Once you use this feature, you can’t use it again until you finish a short or long rest.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
19TH LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Ability Score Improvement (ASI)  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
20TH LEVEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Apex of Patterns
Your skill at perceiving and manipulating reality’s code is unmatched. You become proficient in all saving throws. Additionally, when you use your Disrupt Pattern damage, you can deal maximum damage instead of rolling. Once you use this maximum damage option, you must finish a short or long rest before you can do so again.

Cryptic Archetype Capstone  
You also gain the level 20 capstone feature of your Archetype.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SAMPLE CRYPTIC ARCHETYPES
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Below are three example archetypes that capture typical “Cryptic” themes. Feel free to modify or create your own to suit your campaign’s flavor.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
1) PATTERN BREAKER
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
You specialize in violently unraveling the threads of reality, focusing on direct disruption.

3rd—Shatter Pattern  
When you deal Disrupt Pattern damage, you can cause the target to make a Constitution saving throw (DC = 8 + your proficiency bonus + your Intelligence modifier). On a failure, the target subtracts 1d4 from its next saving throw before the start of your next turn.

7th—Feedback Pulse  
Whenever a creature within 30 feet of you deals damage to you, you can use your reaction to cause it to take psychic damage equal to half the damage it dealt to you, up to your Intelligence modifier (minimum 1). Once you use this feature, you can’t do so again until you finish a short or long rest.

11th—Reality Rend  
As an action, you release a 15-foot cone of disruptive energy. Each creature in the cone must make a Dexterity saving throw (DC as above), taking 4d8 force damage on a failed save, or half as much on a success. Creatures that fail are also staggered, losing reactions until the start of your next turn. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Intelligence modifier (minimum once) before a long rest.

15th—Corrosive Patterns  
When you hit a target with Disrupt Pattern damage, you ignore resistance to psychic or force damage the target may have, and treat immunity as resistance.

20th—Pattern Annihilator  
You can combine your Reality Rend with Shatter Pattern. When you use Reality Rend, the first creature that fails its saving throw automatically fails the Constitution save against your Shatter Pattern. Additionally, your Reality Rend damage increases to 6d8 force damage.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
2) PSYCHE SHAPER
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
You focus on mental illusions and emotional manipulation, shaping minds rather than rending reality.

3rd—Emotional Tweak  
When you hit a creature with Disrupt Pattern damage, you can shift its mood or perceptions. The target makes a Charisma saving throw (DC = 8 + prof. bonus + Int mod). On a failure, you impose one of the following emotional states for 1 minute (or until you choose to end it as a bonus action): fear, fascination, or calm. The effect is subtle but influences the target’s behavior.  

7th—Shared Delusion  
You can cast phantasmal force once without expending a spell slot, using Intelligence as your spellcasting ability. You regain the ability to do so after a short or long rest.

11th—Muddle Mind  
As an action, you can target a creature within 30 feet. The creature must succeed on an Intelligence saving throw or have disadvantage on Intelligence and Wisdom checks for 1 minute. It can repeat the save at the end of each of its turns.

15th—Memory Rewrite  
Once per long rest, you can cast modify memory (using Intelligence as your spellcasting ability) without expending a spell slot. A target that fails its saving throw has no recollection that its mind was altered.

20th—Master of Illusions  
Any time you cast an illusion spell of 5th level or lower, you can choose one target of the spell to automatically fail its initial saving throw against that spell. Additionally, your illusions bypass true seeing and similar effects unless the ability’s user succeeds on a Wisdom saving throw against your spell save DC.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
3) REALITY HACKER
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Specialists in rewriting the “physics” code of the world around them to manipulate terrain, gravity, and space.

3rd—Spatial Distortion  
As a bonus action, you create a 10-foot-radius distortion within 60 feet that remains for 1 minute. Any creature entering the area must spend 2 feet of movement for every 1 foot moved. A creature you choose can ignore this effect. You can move this distortion up to 20 feet as a bonus action on subsequent turns.

7th—Elevate/Depress  
You learn to momentarily alter gravity for a creature within 30 feet. As a bonus action, you force that creature to make a Strength saving throw (DC = 8 + prof. bonus + Int mod). On a failure, you can choose one:  
• The creature is lifted 10 feet in the air and is restrained (hovering) until the start of your next turn.  
• The creature’s speed is halved until the start of your next turn.  

11th—Phase Step  
You can cast blink once without expending a spell slot, using Intelligence as your spellcasting ability. After using Phase Step, you can’t use it again until you finish a short or long rest.

15th—Recode Terrain  
You can spend 1 minute rewriting the physical laws in a 30-foot cube within 60 feet. For the next hour, you can alter up to two of the following in the area:  
• Gravity (normal, halved, or doubled)  
• Terrain difficulty (normal terrain becomes difficult, or vice versa)  
• Visibility (lightly obscured, heavily obscured, or normal)  

20th—Universal Rewrite  
As an action, choose a 60-foot-radius sphere within 120 feet. You can shift that area into the Astral Plane for 1 minute, bringing all creatures in that radius with it (unwilling creatures can make a Charisma saving throw to resist). Within this localized Astral bubble, you and your allies can move creatures and objects at will (though you must maintain concentration, as if on a spell). When it ends, all creatures and objects return to their original positions relative to the wider world.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

ADAPTING TO YOUR GAME
• If you prefer a psionics system instead of standard spellcasting, treat features that reference “spells” as psionic disciplines or talents.  
• If you need to adjust power level, consider shifting some feature prerequisites or reducing the frequency of certain powerful abilities.  
• Be mindful of potential overlap with Rogues, Warlocks, or Wizards who rely on illusions or subtle manipulations. The Cryptic is intended to fill a unique niche with thematic “pattern” flavor.

This completes the suggested homebrew conversion of the Cryptic class for 5e. Always coordinate specific mechanical adjustments with your DM, and feel free to tweak features, spells, or psionic-like abilities to fit the tone and balance of your campaign. Enjoy uncovering (and disrupting) the secret code of reality!

instruction: Please provide some ideas for an interactive reflection assignment on Ethical dilemmas in social media marketing
output:
Below are a few interactive reflection assignment ideas that can help students engage deeply with ethical dilemmas in social media marketing. These activities encourage critical thinking, group collaboration, and personal reflection. You can select or adapt any of these to best fit your class’s size, learning objectives, and mode of delivery.

1) Role-Play Scenarios Laboratory  
• Description: Divide students into small groups and distribute brief case studies or prompts describing common ethical dilemmas in social media marketing (e.g., influencer transparency, user data exploitation, misleading sponsored content). Each group role-plays the scenario, taking on different stakeholder perspectives (marketing firm, influencer, consumer, platform regulations).  
• Process:  
  1. Give each group a scenario card and clearly outline the roles.  
  2. Allow time for group discussions to plan out their viewpoints.  
  3. Invite groups to act out or present their scenarios to the class.  
  4. After each role-play, hold a debrief session for the whole class.  
• Reflection: Ask students to journal their own observations regarding values conflicts, decision-making pressures, or gray areas. Prompt them to consider how their real-life beliefs might influence their professional conduct in similar situations.

2) “Ethical Compass” Debate  
• Description: Split the class into two opposing sides for a structured debate about a controversial social media marketing practice—for instance, micro-targeting ads that exploit user browsing data.  
• Process:  
  1. Provide background readings on the ethical and regulatory frameworks that apply to social media marketing.  
  2. Assign one side to advocate for the practice (highlighting business advantages) and the other to argue against it (emphasizing user rights and privacy).  
  3. Conduct a timed debate, rotating speakers so that multiple students have the opportunity to contribute.  
• Reflection: After the debate, have students write a short reflection explaining whether (or how) their perspective changed and how they might handle these dilemmas as marketing professionals.

3) Create a Social Media Marketing “Code of Ethics”  
• Description: In groups, ask students to collaboratively develop a short, practical “Code of Ethics” document addressing issues such as truthfulness in advertising, respect for user privacy, and transparency in sponsored content.  
• Process:  
  1. Provide examples of existing professional codes (e.g., from the American Marketing Association or PRSA).  
  2. Challenge groups to synthesize these guidelines into a concise, clear policy focused on social media campaigns.  
  3. Ask each group to present their code to the class, explaining the rationale behind their policy choices.  
• Reflection: Have each student submit a one-page individual reflection describing how they might apply this code in real-life marketing scenarios and where they see potential conflicts.

4) Digital Storytelling Exercise  
• Description: Let students create a short digital story (e.g., a brief film, animated infographic, or multimedia presentation) illustrating an ethical dilemma and its potential impact on stakeholders.  
• Process:  
  1. Encourage students to use real-life examples from recent news or personal experiences.  
  2. Include data, visuals, and interviews or simulated interviews to ground the dilemma in real context.  
  3. Have them detail possible outcomes and the moral reasoning behind choosing one course of action over another.  
• Reflection: Students can post their digital stories on a class discussion board, followed by peer reviews. In their reflection, ask them to compare and contrast the ethical perspectives shown in classmates’ stories.

5) “Shadow Marketing” Audit and Reflection  
• Description: Students “audit” their own social media feeds for ads, sponsored content, or influencer posts. They then analyze them for ethical (or questionable) marketing practices.  
• Process:  
  1. Have each student spend a few days documenting every ad or sponsored post they encounter.  
  2. Ask them to note how the content was targeted to them (registrations, browsing history, demographics).  
  3. In small groups, share findings and discuss patterns: Who might be responsible for these ads? Are they transparent about sponsorship? Do they collect or use personal data in ethically questionable ways?  
• Reflection: Students write a reflective essay or post discussing how these observations changed their understanding of common marketing practices. Encourage them to suggest improvements or alternative approaches based on ethical frameworks.

By combining these activities, you can create a semester-long or multi-session exploration of ethical dilemmas in social media marketing. Each idea enables students to interact not only with the core issues but also with their peers’ perspectives, fostering a more robust, well-rounded reflection on professional morality and choices in marketing.

instruction: Can you create a product designed for Sales and Network Marketing Agents. Tell me what the 3 biggest pain points are for people in Sales & Network Marketing. Tell me how our product Solves these 3 biggest pain points. Come up with names for this product. Who is my Target audience for this product and why is it beneficial for them to take action and sign up now?
output:
Below is a structured breakdown of a potential product for Sales and Network Marketing Agents, including the three biggest pain points, how the product solves them, possible product names, the target audience, and why it’s beneficial for them to sign up now.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
1. Three Biggest Pain Points
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
1) Lead Generation & Prospecting Challenges  
   • Agents often struggle to find quality leads on a consistent basis.  
   • They may not have an efficient system for capturing, tracking, and following up with prospects.  

2) Time Management & Overwhelm  
   • Juggling multiple tasks—follow-ups, emails, calls—can be overwhelming and unorganized.  
   • Poor time management leads to missed opportunities and decreased productivity.  

3) Team Building & Retention  
   • In network marketing, building and retaining a high-performing team is a constant challenge.  
   • Agents need tools to motivate, educate, and support team members effectively.  

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
2. Product Solution
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Let’s call the solution a “comprehensive platform” that focuses on three main pillars: Lead Optimizer, Productivity Booster, and Team Accelerator. Each pillar addresses one of the pain points.

   • Team Onboarding & Training Hub: A centralized portal with step-by-step learning modules for new and existing team members.

3. Possible Product Names
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
• “Sales Surge Pro”  
• “Network Nexus”  
• “Peak Performance Suite”
