Below is a simple example of how you might set up a TFTP fuzzer using the Sulley framework. This example focuses on fuzzing TFTP “Read Request” (RRQ) and “Write Request” (WRQ) packets. You can expand upon it to include additional TFTP operations (DATA, ACK, ERROR, etc.) or more complex test cases. 

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DISCLAIMER
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• This example is provided for educational and authorized penetration testing purposes only.  
• Always ensure you have explicit permission to test any systems or services you do not own.  
• Misuse of these techniques could violate the law.  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Install and set up Sulley
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Make sure you have Python 2.7 installed (Sulley is known to have issues with Python 3.x).  
2. Install the Sulley framework. You can clone the repo from GitHub or install from a fork that supports your environment. For example:  
   git clone https://github.com/OpenRCE/sulley.git  
3. Install any additional dependencies needed (e.g., pygraphviz, etc.).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Basic TFTP structure
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TFTP uses UDP (commonly on port 69). The typical packet formats are:  
• RRQ (Read Request) / WRQ (Write Request):  
   ┌───────┬─────────┬───────┬─────────┬───────┐  
   │ Opcode│ Filename│   0   │  Mode   │   0   │  
   └───────┴─────────┴───────┴─────────┴───────┘  
• DATA:  
   ┌───────┬───────┬──────────────┐  
   │ Opcode│ Block │   Data...    │  
   └───────┴───────┴──────────────┘  
• ACK:  
   ┌───────┬───────┐  
   │ Opcode│ Block │  
   └───────┴───────┘  
• ERROR:  
   ┌───────┬───────┬───────────────┬───────┐  
   │ Opcode│  Code │ Error Message │  0    │  
   └───────┴───────┴───────────────┴───────┘  

For our basic example, we’ll fuzz the filename and mode fields in RRQ and WRQ.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Example Sulley script (tftp_fuzzer.py)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

#!/usr/bin/env python2
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-

# Import Sulley modules
from sulley import *

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Define the TFTP packet structure for a Read Request (RRQ) or Write Request (WRQ)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------------
def create_rrq_wrq_structure(opcode_name):
    """
    Creates a basic RRQ/WRQ structure:
      [2-byte Opcode][Filename][0x00][Mode][0x00]
    """
    s_initialize(opcode_name)

    # 2-byte opcode: 1 for RRQ, 2 for WRQ
    # We'll handle them as static fields for clarity, but you could fuzz them too.
    if s_block_start("opcode"):
        if opcode_name == "RRQ":
            s_static("\x00\x01", name="opcode_rrq")
        elif opcode_name == "WRQ":
            s_static("\x00\x02", name="opcode_wrq")
    s_block_end("opcode")

    if s_block_start("filename"):
        # Fuzz the filename
        s_string("testfile.bin", name="filename", max_len=100, fuzzable=True)
    s_block_end("filename")

    # Null terminator for the filename
    s_static("\x00", name="filename_terminator")

    if s_block_start("mode"):
        # Common TFTP modes: "octet", "netascii", "mail"
        # We'll fuzz it with some default seeds
        s_string("octet", name="mode", max_len=20, fuzzable=True)
    s_block_end("mode")

    # Null terminator for the mode
    s_static("\x00", name="mode_terminator")


def main():
    # Initialize the Sulley session
    session_name = "tftp_fuzz_session"
    sess = sessions.session(session_name=session_name)

    # Define our target: TFTP typically listens on UDP port 69
    target = sessions.target("127.0.0.1", 69, proto="udp")

    # Attach the target to the session
    sess.add_target(target)

    # Create our two test cases: one for RRQ, one for WRQ
    create_rrq_wrq_structure("RRQ")
    sess.connect(s_get("RRQ"))

    create_rrq_wrq_structure("WRQ")
    sess.connect(s_get("WRQ"))

    # Start the fuzzing process
    sess.fuzz()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. How this script works
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
• s_initialize creates a new “fuzzable block” in the Sulley framework, which we name ("RRQ" or "WRQ").  
• s_static is used for exact byte values that we don’t want to fuzz here (the opcode).  
• s_string is used for fields (filename and mode) where we do want to fuzz. We provide an initial seed value and allow Sulley to mutate it.  
• The session (sess) manages the fuzz states and test cases.  
• We connect our fuzzable requests to the target on UDP port 69.  
• sess.fuzz() runs through permutations of the data, sending them to the target.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Running the fuzzer
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Ensure that you have a TFTP server running on 127.0.0.1 (or change the IP in the script).  
2. Run your Python 2.x environment: python2 tftp_fuzzer.py  
3. Watch for crashes or unusual behavior on the TFTP server under test.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Potential customizations and improvements
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
• Add additional TFTP message structures (DATA, ACK, ERROR).  
• Expand the fuzzing blocks for mode or other fields (block numbers, error codes, etc.).  
• Integrate Sulley’s monitor/agent implementations to track application crashes (useful for more robust fuzzing).  
• Adjust timeouts, intervals, or thread counts in the session configuration.  
• Implement post-test checks to verify target stability.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ADDITIONAL USAGE NOTES
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• You may need to tailor the wait times or the way Sulley replays payloads, especially since TFTP is connectionless (UDP).  
• Consider setting up network captures (e.g., Wireshark) to verify that you see the traffic you expect.  
• Again, only test on systems and networks that you own or have explicit permission to test.  

This basic example should help you get started on fuzzing TFTP servers with Sulley. You are encouraged to expand upon it with more advanced tests, logging, monitoring, and robust error handling to make your fuzzing engagements more thorough. Good luck and stay within the bounds of authorized security research!

instruction: write a Python function to convert coco format to yolo format
output:
Below is a simple Python function demonstrating how to convert a bounding box in COCO format (x_min, y_min, width, height) into the YOLO format (x_center, y_center, width, height). By default, YOLO expects the coordinates to be normalized by the image dimensions (so that coordinates range from 0 to 1):

def coco_to_yolo(bbox, img_width, img_height):
    """
    Convert a single COCO-format bounding box to YOLO format.

    :param bbox: A list or tuple of 4 values [x_min, y_min, width, height]
                 in COCO format.
    :param img_width: The width of the image.
    :param img_height: The height of the image.
    :return: A list of 4 values [x_center, y_center, width, height]
             in YOLO format, normalized by the image dimensions.
    """
    x_min, y_min, w, h = bbox

    # Calculate center point
    x_center = x_min + (w / 2.0)
    y_center = y_min + (h / 2.0)

    # Normalize by image dimensions
    x_center_norm = x_center / img_width
    y_center_norm = y_center / img_height
    w_norm = w / img_width
    h_norm = h / img_height

    return [x_center_norm, y_center_norm, w_norm, h_norm]

Example usage:

# Example COCO bounding box: (x_min=50, y_min=100, width=150, height=200)
coco_bbox = [50, 100, 150, 200]
image_width = 1280
image_height = 720

yolo_bbox = coco_to_yolo(coco_bbox, image_width, image_height)
print(yolo_bbox)
# possible output (example): [0.09765625, 0.2777777777777778, 0.1171875, 0.2777777777777778]

This gives the YOLO format [x_center, y_center, width, height] all normalized between 0 and 1.

instruction: Write some example scripts on how to interact with YOLO using Python. Focus on batch processing images and saving identified features as tags.
output:
Below are a couple of example Python scripts demonstrating how to perform batch object detection with YOLO and store the detected objects (tags) in a structured form. You can adapt them to your specific use case, such as saving results into a database, a CSV file, or simply logging them in a JSON-like format. 

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1) Using YOLOv5 via PyTorch Hub
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Prerequisites:
• pip install torch torchvision torchaudio  
• Optional: pip install opencv-python (for image loading/display)  
• The PyTorch Hub will automatically download the ultralytics/yolov5 repository and the required model.

Code example (batch_inference_yolov5.py):

------------------------------------------------------------
import os
import csv
import torch
import cv2

def load_images_from_folder(folder_path):
    """Load image file paths from a given folder."""
    image_files = []
    for file_name in os.listdir(folder_path):
        if file_name.lower().endswith(('.png', '.jpg', '.jpeg')):
            image_files.append(os.path.join(folder_path, file_name))
    return image_files

def run_batch_inference(folder_path, output_csv='yolo_output.csv'):
    """
    Run object detection on all images in a folder using YOLOv5 
    (via PyTorch Hub) and save detected tags in a CSV file.
    """

    # Load YOLOv5s model from PyTorch Hub (pretrained on COCO dataset)
    model = torch.hub.load('ultralytics/yolov5', 'yolov5s', pretrained=True)

    # Collect all images
    image_paths = load_images_from_folder(folder_path)
    print(f"Found {len(image_paths)} images to process.")

    # Run inference in batches
    batch_size = 16  # Adjust batch size based on your GPU/CPU memory
    results_list = []

    for i in range(0, len(image_paths), batch_size):
        batch_files = image_paths[i : i + batch_size]

        # Load images into a list (OpenCV or PIL)
        batch_images = [cv2.cvtColor(cv2.imread(f), cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB) for f in batch_files]
        
        # Inference
        results = model(batch_images)

        # Each image's detections are stored separately
        for file_path, pred in zip(batch_files, results.xyxy):
            # pred is a 2D tensor (one row per detected object):
            # Each row has: [x1, y1, x2, y2, confidence, class_index]
            # results.names[class_index] gives the class name
            image_name = os.path.basename(file_path)
            for *box, conf, cls_idx in pred.tolist():
                label = results.names[int(cls_idx)]
                x1, y1, x2, y2 = box
                results_list.append([image_name, label, conf, x1, y1, x2, y2])

    # Write results to a CSV file
    with open(output_csv, mode='w', newline='', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        writer = csv.writer(f)
        writer.writerow(['Image', 'Label', 'Confidence', 'X1', 'Y1', 'X2', 'Y2'])
        writer.writerows(results_list)
    
    print(f"Inference complete. Results saved to {output_csv}")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    folder_path = 'path/to/images'
    run_batch_inference(folder_path)
------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation:
• load_images_from_folder scans a specified folder and collects all valid image paths.  
• run_batch_inference loads a pretrained YOLOv5s model, splits the images into batches, and runs inference on each batch.  
• results.xyxy is a list where each element corresponds to one of the input images; each element is a tensor of shape Nx6, containing bounding boxes, confidence, and class indices.  
• We use results.names to map a class index (e.g., 0 for “person”) to its string label (e.g., “person”).  
• The final output is saved to a CSV file with bounding box coordinates, predicted labels, and confidence scores.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2) Using YOLOv8 via the ultralytics library
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Prerequisites:
• pip install ultralytics opencv-python  

Code example (batch_inference_yolov8.py):

------------------------------------------------------------
import os
import csv
import cv2
from ultralytics import YOLO

def load_images_from_folder(folder_path):
    """Load image file paths from a given folder."""
    image_files = []
    for file_name in os.listdir(folder_path):
        if file_name.lower().endswith(('.png', '.jpg', '.jpeg')):
            image_files.append(os.path.join(folder_path, file_name))
    return image_files

def run_batch_inference(folder_path, output_csv='yolov8_output.csv'):
    """
    Run object detection on all images in a folder using YOLOv8
    and save detected tags in a CSV file.
    """

    # Load YOLOv8 model (pretrained on COCO dataset)
    model = YOLO('yolov8n.pt')  # or 'yolov8m.pt', 'yolov8l.pt', etc.

    # Collect all images
    image_paths = load_images_from_folder(folder_path)
    print(f"Found {len(image_paths)} images to process.")

    # Results list to store each detection
    results_list = []

    # Process images (the model can handle a list of file paths or numpy arrays)
    results = model.predict(image_paths, save=False, imgsz=640, conf=0.25)

    # Parse results
    for file_path, result in zip(image_paths, results):
        image_name = os.path.basename(file_path)
        
        # result.boxes contains all predictions for this image
        # Each box has .xyxy (bounding box), .conf (confidence), and .cls (class index)
        for box in result.boxes:
            x1, y1, x2, y2 = box.xyxy[0].tolist()
            conf = float(box.conf[0])
            cls_idx = int(box.cls[0])
            label = result.names[cls_idx]  # class name
            results_list.append([image_name, label, conf, x1, y1, x2, y2])

    # Write results to a CSV file
    with open(output_csv, mode='w', newline='', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        writer = csv.writer(f)
        writer.writerow(['Image', 'Label', 'Confidence', 'X1', 'Y1', 'X2', 'Y2'])
        writer.writerows(results_list)

    print(f"Inference complete. Results saved to {output_csv}")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    folder_path = 'path/to/images'
    run_batch_inference(folder_path)
------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation:
• YOLO('yolov8n.pt') loads a lightweight YOLOv8 model (YOLOv8 Nano). You can choose a different model weight file if desired.  
• model.predict(image_paths) processes all the images in a single call. The output is a list of results, one for each input image.  
• result.boxes contains bounding boxes, confidence scores, and class indices. We use result.names to map the class index to the string label.  
• The final step writes everything to a CSV file so that you can follow up with analytics, or import it into another system.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Additional Notes / Tips
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Confidence Threshold: Adjust the confidence threshold (e.g., conf=0.25) to filter out low-confidence detections.  
• Batch Size: Depending on your hardware memory, you may increase or decrease the batch size (for YOLOv5 PyTorch Hub usage, you can split images manually into chunks). YOLOv8’s .predict() handles batching internally.  
• Output Formats:  
  – Instead of CSV, you can store results in JSON.  
  – Or directly save results into a database.  
• Speed/Performance: Consider GPU acceleration if available (CUDA). For CPU-only systems, reduce the image size (imgsz) or use a smaller model for faster inference.  
• Visualization: You can draw bounding boxes on the images using OpenCV if you want to visually inspect the predictions:  
  cv2.rectangle(image, (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (0,255,0), 2)  

These examples should help you get started performing batch inference with YOLO models in Python and saving the detected objects as tags or metadata for your downstream applications. Feel free to expand upon these scripts to suit your specific workflow or data-processing pipeline.
